subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS

speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, June 24, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the second reading of Bill No. 80, to amend the National Resources Mobilization Act, 1940, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Roy.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this has been a very long debate. Almost every point of view on economic and social questions has been aired in this house, and I think it is only fair to say to my friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that the conscription of wealth is now an inescapable reality. I do not think there is much more to conscript; wealth is down the drain. I would make this short statement, however. I do believe that in the post-war period we shall have this country so organized that we irhall be in a position to abolish want.
Opinions have been expressed indicating the will of the Canadian people on the plebiscite. There is no doubt in my mind that our people definitely placed the responsibility upon parliament and the government to implement any policy including conscription for overseas service if they deemed it necessary for the successful prosecution of the war. It has brought to the surface the driving force of the faith in the future destiny of this country, and the fundamental viewpoints of those in favour of and those opposed to conscription of men for service overseas. I would point out to some who have taken part in the debate that some of the arguments used have been prevalent in countries which have long since fallen under the heel of the enemy, whose people are now suffering from the mistakes of their leaders.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Mitchell
This war is different from the last war. In the last war the front was mainly in continental Europe and the allies had almost unchallenged control of the seas. In this war the front encircles the globe and their control of the seas is by no means sure. In the last war our problem was how soon the allies would win; in this war the problem has always been and still is whether we can stave off defeat long enough to enable us effectively to mobilize our man-power and our resources on behalf of the common front of the united nations. In the last war our defeat would have meant some loss of territory and possibly the payment of an indemnity, but even after defeat we would have continued to lead our own lives with the loss of only a few of our liberties. In this war, as the experience of all the conquered nations shows, defeat means the utter and ruthless repression of all our liberties and our institutions and the degradation of all of us to the level of slaves and beasts of burden to the master race.
Let us visualize the position in which we are in this dominion at the moment. Eleven million people are living on what is almost a continent, and by the same token one of the richest parts of the world. Through the genius and foresight of our people we have pushed back the arctic circle so that we can grow things where they had never grown before. We have uncovered mineral riches which have added greatly to our productive powers and without which successful war cannot be waged. As I have already pointed out, we are a small population living in a vast country; but on the basis of our ability to produce the instruments of war, the valour of our fighting men, and the initiative of those engaged in industrial and agricultural pursuits, we are a far more important unit of the united nations than mere population would indicate.
We have heard it said in this house, and also outside, that Canada is not on a total war footing, the inference being that without conscription for overseas service we cannot wage total war. What is total war? Does it mean squeezing the last possible man out of the population and putting him in uniform, or does it mean making the maximum war effort by a balanced distribution of man-power between the armed services on the one hand, and, on the other, agriculture, war industry and civilian occupations? We may well ask ourselves these questions. Hon. members' memories are not so short that they cannot recall the words of Prime Minister Churchill, "Give us the tools and we will finish the job."

It cannot be denied that Canada has moved with the utmost speed to provide the tools of war on every possible front. My colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) indicated this in a striking manner to the house the other day. This war cannot be won with bows and arrows. Dunkirk, Hong Kong, Singapore, Purma, and more recently Tobruk, should have taught us the folly of raising men for armed forces without also providing them with the best and most powerful weapons of war. Let this be clearly understood: we must maintain the level of our war production to ensure the adequate provision of war equipment for our own men and those of the united nations, but we must soon face the question, how long we can continue to increase both the number of our men in the armed forces and war production.
As one of the major arsenals and granaries in the British commonwealth, our Canadian war problem resolves itself primarily into a balance for the allocation of total man- and woman-power to:	(1) the armed services;
(2) production of munitions; (3) production of foodstuffs for war purposes; (4) production of essential civilian supplies. While raising a large number of men for the armed services, we have been able at the same time to achieve a remarkable increase in both industrial and agricultural production. Up to the present we have been able to accomplish this by a process of natural selection, allowing individuals to. find that war-time service in which they feel able to make their best contribution to the total war effort. However, the time has come when we cannot reach the military, industrial and agricultural goals that are necessary to ensure victory without the gradual exercise of some government direction and control. One has only to read the newspapers-and by this I do not necessarily mean editorials. In recent issues of the Toronto and Ottawa papers I have noted almost frantic appeals from war industry for men. Many of these industries are located in ridings represented by hon. members here this afternoon, and they cover almost the whole field of human endeavour. Particularly is there need for men in the heavy industries; and in my judgment, if we are to continue production on the scale on which we are now producing-and of course we have planned for even a further increased production-it will be necessary to pay particular attention to heavy industry, because it is the basic industry of the war, in which few women can be employed. I believe that steps will have to be taken in the very near future to see that the heavy industries of this country are provided with sufficient men

Mobilization Act-Mr. Mitchell
so that we can produce the necessary supplies according to plan. I sometimes wonder whether we have not tried to do too much for a nation the size of ours.
In recent weeks I have received many visits from industrialists who are anxious about the shortage of labour and its effect on war production. I should like to quote two paragraphs from a letter which, because of the nature of its contents, dealing with the war effort, was confidential. This paragraph reads:
Indications are that this condition is going to become worse, since we have a number of production units which will go into production during the summer months, so that unless more labour becomes available by the fall our efficiency will be greatly impaired.
At the present time we have need for between 300 and 400 men, and with the new units going into production we will require by September or October a force of approximately 500 to 600 more than the number we now have working. We are doing everything we can to relieve the situation by picking up labour in the north country and in various other parts of Ontario where we understand non-essential industry is being curtailed.
I could instance many other appeals for labour to take jobs on which women cannot be employed. It is evident that almost all our people who are ordinarily accepted for work in industry and agriculture are now fully employed. From now on we must carefully classify the man- and woman-power of the country so that every individual can be referred to the work in which he can make his maximum contribution to our war effort.
The conclusion is inescapable that we cannot reach the military, industrial and agricultural goal which we must attain to ensure victory without steadily increasing resort to measures of government direction and control, of which I now wish to speak briefly.
Effective utilization of man-power implies that none be wasted by unemployment. Every unemployed male worker is now required to register for work and to keep that registration active as long as he remains unemployed. This will soon be made compulsory for women workers also. It is generally agreed that every effort should be made to offer jobs first to the available men. We do not expect 100 per cent success in removing every local or temporary pocket of unemployment; even Great Britain has not been able to achieve that. But lack of success will no longer be because of incomplete information. We must know of every unemployed worker, where he is and what sort of work he is best fitted for.
On Friday last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) requested a statement as to the total numbers of males and females recorded at the employment offices across Canada in
compliance with the order requiring all male persons from sixteen to sixty-nine years of age to register. I may say that the employment offices have been reporting the number of persons who at specified dates had applied for work and who on the dates reported had not yet been placed. The following are comparative figures, as at April 30 in the years 1940, 1941 and 1942, of those who had voluntarily come to the employment offices seeking work and have not been placed:

However, the comparison I have just given of unplaced applicants as between 1940 and 1942 shows that the reservoir of available labour is almost entirely depleted.
An interesting check against the foregoing figures is disclosed by the employment reports secured monthly by the bureau of statistics from firms employing more than fifteen employees. These reports indicate a very large increase in the number of persons employed in non-agricultural employment. The figures are:

It is apparent from these figures that the number of persons reporting voluntarily for work is decreasing rapidly and that the number of persons employed in this group of roughly 13,000 firms has increased by over a million in the last two years.
It is interesting to note that in April, 1942, as compared with April, 1940, the number of unplaced applicants at the employment offices showed a decrease of 74 per cent and the number of wage earners employed by these 13,000 firms had increased between March, 1940, and March, 1942, by 47 per cent.
It was our opinion that the number of employable men who have not registered at the offices voluntarily was very small. However to make sure and to obtain a registration of employable women on a voluntary basis and generally to encourage the use of the employment offices, compulsory registration of men and voluntary registration of women

Mobilization Act-Mr. Mitchell
was ordered to be taken, early in June. At the close of business on June 11, 1942, as a result of the two registrations the total number reported as being unemployed in Canada was:
Women	 8,818
Men	 59,933
Total	 68,751
It should be noted that the number of women who registered is not greatly in excess of the figures for April 30, 1942. Since the registration was voluntary, most of those who registered were women who were actually seeking employment. As the registration of men was compulsory, the 59,933 who registered included many unemployable persons, many only partly employable and many who for various reasons it would be difficult to place in employment. The employment officers are examining the registration, and from preliminary but incomplete returns it appears that some 50 per cent of the 59,933 males are totally or partly unemployable. Accordingly the net figure of employable men registered is approximately the same as the total number of males who had voluntarily registered at April 30, 1942, or something over 20,000, and not more than 30,000 unplaced on June 11, 1942. This is a remarkably low figure, undoubtedly an all-time low for Canada. The registration of all those persons covered by unemployment insurance is almost complete. They are being classified by age, skill, sex, and industry.
It is obvious that we cannot meet our manpower requirements solely from the present small number of unemployed. Women must replace men in very many occupations within the range of their strength and skill; men must be transferred from less essential to more essential industry, and it may be necessary further to contract employment in less essential production. One has only to walk down the main streets of any of our cities to observe that we have not yet touched the fringe of the measure of sacrifice necessary for victory.
One will appreciate the difficulties in establishing a man-power inventory when we are dealing with the records of millions of individuals. The inventory gets out of date before it can be put to effective use. But we are undertaking to maintain a running inventory of our man-power by requiring employers to report all additions to and separations from their payrolls. This is essential to reduce excessive and wasteful labour turnover. The effort to prohibit enticement from war industries was not effective, because employers were free to hire anybody who applied. How-

ever, the wage control policy has restrained employers from putting up wages in their competition for scarce labour. This competition, of course, did not increase the total supply of labour, but simply caused more movement of the available supply between employers.
We intend to channel all transfers of labour through employment offices. At the moment employers are required to notify the national selective service officer of all their vacancies and all prospective lay-offs, and they may engage only persons referred to them or approved by the national selective service officer. This is the beginning of genuine control and direction of man-power. The national selective service officer, as the system develops, will have before him at all times the local demand for and the supply of labour.
As employers and employees grow more accustomed to using the officers, and as the officers gradually learn the details of their local situations, it will be possible, either generally or in particular localities, or in respect of particular industries and occupations, to tighten or slacken the control as circumstances necessitate. This will mean some inconvenience to both employers and employees. A tremendous burden of work and responsibility is imposed on the employment offices, but the procedure if effective will facilitate post-war readjustments in employment of untold ben-fit and value.
The house is well aware of the steps already taken with respect to the maintenance of an adequate labour supply for agriculture. I would like to say this to my farmer and industrial friends. This war in its very essence demands that we improvise from day to day, and as the changing conditions require, the measures necessary to free men for the fighting forces so that victory may be assured.
Last year the province of Ontario, in cooperation with the dominion, was able to organize a farm labour programme that provided an additional 23,000 workers to assist in the peak period of agricultural activities, and a similar arrangement has been made for this year.
It is certain that governments cannot do everything, but I am confident that with the intelligent cooperation of the farmers themselves most of the difficulties of farm labour supply can be minimized.
If I had more time I could discuss the war emergency training programme under which tens of thousands have been trained, and the plan recently adopted to train 15,000 war plant job instructors within a period of three months. We have set in motion, in cooperation with the universities, a course of training

Mobilization Act-Mr. Mitchell
in personnel work, because of the dearth of qualified men in that field, which I think will be of untold benefit both to employers and to employees in our industrial life. From my experience as chairman of the industrial disputes inquiry commission I am of the opinion that one great defect is the lack of knowledge by some managements of how to deal with the human element in industry. A man may be one of the brightest of engineers, but when it comes to the engineering of men he sometimes is the worst kind of engineer, and we have felt in the labour department that with the development of a personnel force especially trained and skilled in the handling of men much unnecessary industrial friction may be avoided. The British government have taken similar steps, also our friends to the south.
We have arranged with the universities and the provinces to provide assistance to student doctors, dentists, engineers, and scientists who on graduation will be directed to the armed services and war industries. This financial aid will make it possible to continue the courses in the summer months and will speed up training in these most important occupations.
Funds are being made available to meet the transportation costs of moving workers to distant employment.
Negotiations are proceeding with the provinces with a view to the conclusion of agreements for the establishment of day nurseries for the children of women employed in the war industries.
It will be observed that by the adoption of a variety of measures, some still in their early stages, the mobilization of Canadian man-power has been proceeding steadily. The regional and national war labour boards are turning to the problems of wage adjustments necessary to attract and retain labour in distant and isolated undertakings, such as the defence projects in British Columbia.
As the labour supply situation tightens I shall be prepared to recommend, and I know the Canadian people would wish me to recommend, whatever measures of increased direction, compulsion or control prove necessary to meet future requirements. As Minister of Labour I have the task of seeing that there are enough men for our war industries. Hence the setting up of the national selective service branch under Mr. Elliott M. Little, who with his associates are moving faster in the total mobilization of man-power than [DOT]many realize. It is the part of statesmanship in this time to unify the people of this dominion so that our national war effort may reach maximum proportions and efficiency. We 44501-233
cannot maintain our free institutions in these desperate times unless there is national unity. I believe that is the soundest policy to pursue.
May I say this, Mr. Speaker, that I am doing many things to-day which are in direct contradiction of everything I have ever believed in, and I am doing them because I believe they are in the interests of this dominion. Many "shalls" and "shall nots" are going out from the Department of Labour every day in the week, but I trust that it may be said of the Minister of Labour and of the government of this country that no step that we take will endanger the liberties that have been handed down to us, and I hope that at the conclusion of the war we shall speedily return to that way of life where the utmost amount of freedom is possible for the people of this country.
Tribute has been paid to the various racial groups that go to make up the life of this dominion. Basically we have French and British, but we have taken within our blood streams most of the finest races of Europe and have fashioned a nation based on the concept of freedom equal to that of any other country in the world.
Mention has been made of imperialism. The British people, and I speak now in the broader sense, with all their faults, have been mainly responsible for the form of government that has made possible even this debate in the House of Commons. It has been my privilege, Mr. Speaker, to visit almost every part of what is sometimes called the British empire, and I know something of the contributions that have been made to democratic government and justice by the British people. I have also seen things and conditions that I felt were not warranted in any civilized country, but viewed in the broad sweep of history I think it will be said that the contributions made by the British empire have been the greatest in the history of the world.
Members of this house have a terrible responsibility. It is their duty to give leadership to their constituents. Freedom, as we understand it, is in the balance. When the history of our time is written, may it be said that we measured up to our responsibility, and that nothing we should have done, no matter what the cost, was not undertaken to preserve the heritage of liberty handed down to us by those who have gone before.
I do not want hon. members to have any doubt as to where I stand on the question of conscription for overseas service. It has been indicated in certain quarters that I am a con-scriptionist. Be that as it may, I hope it can never be said I am not a realist. I want to say in conclusion that when in my view con-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bruce

scription for overseas service is essential to the safety of the state and the preservation of our way of life, I will express my opinion in no uncertain terms.
In conclusion I should like to quote from a book written by an American. It is called "The White Cliffs", and from it I take this thought:
I am American bred,
I have seen much to hate here-much to forgive,
But in a world where England is finished and dead,
I do not wish to live.
That expresses my sentiments.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) upon the excellent speech he has made this afternoon. I take to myself a good deal of credit for the fact that he occupies his present position. Some hon. members will recall that nearly two years ago I recommended to the house that we have as Minister of Labour a man who understood the problems of labour. I am glad to see that for some little time we have had a man as able as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat.
After listening to the monotonous, partisan repetitions of set phrases which came to us like a gramophone record of their master's voice, in the form of speeches by one cabinet minister after another in support of voluntary enlistment, and of the Prime Minister's policy of procrastination in so far as the real issue is concerned, it was indeed refreshing to hear the well-reasoned argument of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) in favour of conscription.
There is no misunderstanding his language when he says:
The need for conscripting those men-
For overseas.
-having arisen, I say frankly . . . the government should have power to apply conscription.
He does not follow the Prime Minister's ifs and whens, or the Minister of National War Services' confessions of an ex-pacifist, but says with conviction that the time is here -now. I congratulate him upon his courage, and the valuable contribution he has made to the debate.
On Tuesday last I listened with much interest to the important speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston). I congratulate him upon the change which has taken place in his attitude toward the manpower problem since he rebuked me in the house following my speech on May 12, 1941, when I had the termerity to suggest the

adoption of compulsory selective service. I admit at once that he may have done this from the very best of motives, knowing as he probably did the effect which even the suggestion of conscription would have upon Quebec. I am glad to find that he now declares there is nothing sinister about the word conscription, and that if it comes to a choice between national unity and national security he will select the latter.
On May 12 I spoke in part as follows:
We should have the compulsory selective service which was visualized by the sweeping powers of the National Resources Mobilization Act passed last June, without the hamstringing clause that prevents men who train under that act from being used wherever the need is urgent. Voluntary recruiting has reached the stage where it is slow, cumbersome and wasteful. I am certain that all parts of Canada will respond to the high patriotic call that the situation now requires. Selective compulsory enlistment is the only fair and efficient way to meet the complex needs of Canada. I venture to suggest therefore that this session should not close until we have disposed of this urgent business.
I objected then, as I do now, and as I did in 1940 when the National Resources Mobilization Act was passed, to section 3 being incorporated in the act. I am firmly of the opinion that if the government had courageously introduced conscription at that time, the province of Quebec would have accepted it, and to-day we would have greater national unity. This lack of unity I attribute to the vacillating leadership we have had under the present government.
From listening to various speeches one would assume that the need for conscription has not yet arisen, but that when it comes- and not until then-conscription will be enforced. They seem to lose sight of the fact that it takes from nine months to two years to make an efficient soldier. When the need comes we cannot just go out and grab men, put them into the service and rush them into the firing line. We have had many illustrations of the lack of wisdom of that procedure.
I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) upon the courage he has shown in casting aside at least temporarily his partisan ties, and upon the able way in which he disposed of the irrelevancies with which the speeches of his political friends have confused the issue. He has offered a correct and logical interpretation of the meaning of the "yes" and "no" votes as applied to conscription. I agree entirely with the hon. member when he says:
The question of conscription cries out for decision, and can no longer be evaded. Let us

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bruce
determine it now. This is the debate, and now is the time. It has already been decided by the high court of the electorate.
And I may say to the hon. member that it was decided by the high court of the electorate in my constituency, as well as in his.
May I also congratulate the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Gray) upon the admirable speech on conscription he delivered in the house on June 18. He expressed the views held by over 80 per cent of the people of this province, and earned their admiration for his courage in doing so. After all, I submit that in time of war, national defence should be placed before party, and that is just what the hon. members to whom I have referred have done.
The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard), speaking yesterday, called for unity and understanding and referred to what he termed the disgusting prejudice against French Canadians. I may tell him that that does not apply to any of the hon. members of this house who are associated with me here. It certainly does not apply to me. I have always advocated tolerance. I should like to quote from a speech I made on April 24, 1934, on our heritage of tolerance. I said:
The priceless heritage of tolerance, the priceless gift of freedom which this dominion, as a part of a great empire holds in trust for this and future generations, will, I know, never be betrayed, never be lost. For it is in this freedom, this tolerance, this true democracy, that the richest life is to be found for all men.
I may tell him also that I have nothing but the kindliest feeling of friendship and admiration for the race which he represents. Many years ago I went to Paris to take a post-graduate course in surgery, because in that city there were some of the most expert exponents of surgery to be found anywhere in the world. I should like to pay a tribute to that great scientist Louis Pasteur, whose discovery that minute organisms caused suppuration has enabled such great progress to be made in surgery. Had it not been for his discovery, many of the successful operations now performed on various parts of the human body would not have been possible.
I believe also that our French-Canadian compatriots are just as loyal as any of us. If they are placed in a false position to-day it is not their fault; it is owing entirely to the perverse education they have received at the hands of the politicians. It is a fact that a million French-Canadian people of Quebec origin who now live in the New England states have responded to the national selective service draft as loyally as any other United States citizens. Our French-Canadian compat-44561-2331
riots would do the same under the leadership of a Roosevelt or a Churchill. Instead they have been misled for political party considerations by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and some of his colleagues. It is clear that the present unhappy situation in Quebec has been due to the spread of anti-British propaganda over a period of years by politicians for their own partisan ends.
The hon. member for Bellechasse has been less than fair in quoting only the statements made by Mr. Asquith in 1915 and 1916, because it was in the latter year that Mr. Asquith was deposed from leadership for his persistence in those views and for following of a policy of "wait and see." There is ample evidence of disunity in this house, as well as a steadily mounting feeling of distrust and despair throughout the country under our present Asquithian leadership, to warn the Prime Minister that he will soon meet a similar fate. I should like to bring the hon. member for Bellechasse up to date by quoting a few passages from a speech made by Mr. Churchill in May, 1939, to be found at page 170 of "Blood, Sweat and Tears." Speaking of the conscription act, he said:
But there is nothing undemocratic about this measure; it is the most democratic thing we have ever done in the islaud. Provided that no exceptions are allowed, it will wear away differences between class and class, and it may also be the beginning of a far more broadly and evenly based society than we have ever known.
And again:
This is a time when prejudices must be abandoned on either side, and a true comradeship established between all parties and classes throughout our loyal anxious land.
Referring to the period of which my hon. friend spoke, he says in part:
This proved intolerable to the national sense of justice. Moreover, the two million households and families whose menfolk had borne the whole burden, were infuriated by the fact that there were very large numbers of perfectly fit men remaining at home, filling at higher wages the jobs of those who had volunteered. It was this sense of wrong and injustice, which spread through the country in the spring and summer of 1916, that alone carried the conscription bill.
How different now! Today, before a shot has been fired, in cool blood we are taking this momentous step, and taking it with a very large measure of national acceptance. Nothing could more vividly mark the manner in which the wage-earning classes-without whom no armies can be formed-have realized the deadly nature of the assault which is being directed at their fundamental right and liberties. What nearly two years of bloody war only attained with difficulty in 1916, is now practically conceded by the will of the nation in a time of nominal peace. This is the point which should impress foreign countries, and-
36S8

Mobilization Act-Mr. Bruce
I interject, "Canada".
-because it is the most explicit guarantee of the resolve of the British people to bear its part in what is now plainly a world cause.
I am sure we were all greatly touched by the pathetic evidence of fog which surrounded the statesman from Saskatchewan when he visited a valley in British Columbia many years ago. One can only conclude that the same fog has pursued him through the years and still envelops him. This is perhaps the kindest way to explain his willingness to sit silent and listen to the aspersions which have been cast upon his former colleague, Bight Hon. Arthur Meighen, in connection with the enforcement of conscription. This would seem to be the appropriate time to get the record straight. Mr. Meighen drew up the conscription act of 1917 in his capacity as Solicitor General, and no one can read that act without agreeing that it is as fair and equitable as a law could be made. All decisions to be made under it with respect to the liberty of the subject were made by impartially appointed tribunals. The bill was introduced by Sir Robert Borden on June 11, 1917. It passed on July 24 of the same year, when it received the practically unanimous support not only of the Conservative members of the house but of a large part of the Liberal party as well. About a month later, on August 28, Mr. Meighen left the justice department to become Secretary of State. On October 2 of the same year he became Minister of the Interior, which position he held until 1919. Sir Robert Borden promised not to give the bill effect until it was submitted to the people in a general election, which was held on December 17, 1917. The actual call for service was not made until January 3, 1918.
The administration of the military service act was entirely under the Department of Justice, whose head was the Hon. C. J. Doherty, of Quebec. From what I can learn there does not appear to have been any complaint at all about its having been unjustly administered, although, doubtless, minor errors were made. The talk, therefore, about the administration of the act being the cause of the opposition is absurd. The opposition, clearly, was to conscription itself, as everybody will realize who has sat in this house during the last week or so.
The present Prime Minister and his Quebec ministers capitalized on it in the most ruthless way. It will be apparent how unfair and untrue it was for the Prime Minister to announce over the radio in seeking the "yes" vote, as he did, as follows:
The pledge not to impose conscription, as everybody knows, was the result of Canada's

experience in the last war. The way in which conscription was then introduced and the way it was enforced gave rise to bitter resentment.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that this statement is the more reprehensible because it was made in what the Prime Minister proclaimed as a non-party campaign, and when Mr. Meighen, a member of the government of 1918, had no means of replying to the audience which the Prime Minister reached, gratis, over the radio.
May I point out that the present Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar) and all the Liberal ministers in the Union government at that time, as well as Mr. Meighen, were jointly responsible for what was done. The minister of mines, who has been a member of the present government for many years, had exactly the same relation to the enforcement of conscription as had Mr. Meighen. But the Liberals made a bogeyman of Mr. Meighen because he became the leader of the Conservative party. If there was anything wrong or unjust in the enforcement of the act, the minister of mines had the full responsibility that Mr. Meighen had, but had not the common fairness between man and man to defend either himself or his former colleague. Instead, he proposes sending me -and other critics of the government to a concentration camp- which only confirms the fears of some people that we are soon to have, if we have not already, a dictatorship in this country. In fact, does not the announcement yesterday of the action launched against Colonel Drew point in the same direction?

I thought the minister's
actions portrayed a little more than a kindly interest. Perhaps not; I am sorry if I misunderstood him. Mr. Churchill says:
There is an extraordinary contrast between the processes of thought and methods of management required in war and those which serve in peace. Much is gained in peace by ignoring or putting off disagreeable or awkward questions, and avoiding clear-cut decisions which, if they please some, offend others. It is often better in peace to persist for a time patiently in an obscure and indeterminate course of action rather than break up or dangerously strain a political combination. ... In war everything is different. There is no place for compromise in war. That invaluable process only means that soldiers are shot because their leaders in council and camp are unable to resolve. In war, the clouds never blow over; they gather unceasingly and fall in thunderbolts. Things do not get better by being let alone; unless they are adjusted they explode with shattering detonation. Clear leadership, violent action, rigid decisions one way or the other, form the only path not only of victory, but of safety and even of mercy.
The state cannot afford division or hesitation at the executive centre. To humour a distinguished man, to avoid a fierce dispute, nay. even to preserve the governing instrument itself, cannot, except as an alternative to sheer anarchy, be held to justify half measures. The peace of the council may for the moment be won, but the price is paid on the battlefield by brave men marching forward against unspeakable terrors in the belief that conviction and coherence have animated their orders.
Thus does Britain's great war-time leader set forth in clear and unmistakable language the distinction between peace and war-time leadership, and confirm the attitude which I took shortly after I entered this house when I raised the question, in all good faith, I submit, whether the qualities that commended our present Prime Minister for the job of conventional statecraft in peace-time were not the very ones which condemned him as a courageous war-time leader. At the time I assured the house, as I do now. that this appraisal of the Prime Minister's ability and temperament was not meant to be personal criticism of him as a man of opposite political faith, because, as I have often said before, I do not consider in these grave times that a man's political viewpoint is of any moment whatever. However, my statement
Mobilization Act-Mr, Bruce

that I was apprehensive as to whether the Prime Minister's temperament was such as to qualify him to direct this nation in the greatest crisis in its history was interpreted falsely, and of course the heavy guns of partisanship were trained on me. May I ask again with equal sincerity if the events of the past weeks do not in some degree justify the apprehension which I expresed two years ago.
Briefly, the Prime Minister's philosophy to keep the party afloat and lie at anchor in the stream of time has not worked even sUcessfully for the great party which he has the honour to head. I further submit that this policy of evasion of responsibility has worked disastrously also for the interests of the nation. Without dealing in recriminations, I should like to say that those of us who, from the most honest and honourable motives, tried to prevent the Prime Minister and his party from evading responsibility by submitting the question of mobilization of manpower, to the people in the form of a plebiscite have been fully justified in opposing this method an the floor of the house. I should like also to add that once the plebiscite as a means had pased this parliament and become an instrument through which the nation was to express its views on mobilization of man-power, I, and the other loyal members of this house, shared equally and vigorously in the campaign to bring the vote on this evasively-worded question to a successful result.
It is with some pride that I point to my constituency, Parkdale in Toronto, and to the result which they gave-92 per cent "yes" in answer to the question which was asked. Speaking as a member from the province of Ontario, I wish to say that the result of the vote in that section of Canada is a magnificent tribute to the patriotism and soundness of the Canadian people. However, the plebiscite is past history. That it was a political blunder of the first magnitude goes without saying. The vote, however, established clearly for this government that there is a division of opinion in Canada on the question of conscription. No matter in what innocuous language the question was phrased, the result of the vote was a clear-cut indication to this government that the people went to the polls and voted on conscription, "yes" or "no".
What is the result? In one part of Canada the carefully nurtured bogey of conscription has borne full and devastating fruit, while throughout the nation as a whole a substantial majority of the people have told this parliament through its government to

introduce full-out conscription and have done with this hypocrisy. In the eyes of world opinion the government's unwillingness in the past to face up to this issue honestly and courageously has done us untold harm. This nation won its reputation and carried influence in world affairs far beyond what its small population justified, because of the magnificent achievements of the Canadian forces in the last war. That this reputation and our current effort have been done serious harm throughout the world by the government's policy of conscription, is an unchallengeable statement. This damage is such that only time and deeds can repair it.
Therefore I appeal to the Prime Minister of this nation, even at this late date. Let us have finished with half measures and deception. Let us obey the will of the majority of the people of this great dominion. Let us put ourselves on an equal plane with the other members of the united nations by a straightforward clear-cut introduction of complete selective compulsory service. I hear our present system defended because the voluntary form of enlistment is said to be successful. I submit it is most niggardly and cowardly for this nation to continue a system which obviously brings out all its best and bravest, placing a penalty on patriotism while paying a premium to the shirkers who stay at home. We all as members of this highest court of the nation stand here as trustees for those brave young flyers, those gallant members of our naval forces, and the yet unproven but equally fine mettle of Canadian manhood which constitutes our active army. Let us be faithful to that trust.
I ask the Prime Minister to amend the present bill in committee to provide for the immediate introduction of conscription. He will perhaps draw strength partly from his political adversaries. If there is a defection on the part of his cultivated followers I am sure it will be accompanied with regrets, but I am equally certain that as this war progresses the wisdom of that course will be vindicated and those who temporarily do not see fit to support a policy of honesty and courage will some day thank him for performing what must be considered the first duty of the head of any government, that of taking the proper steps to protect the lives and property of the people who constitute the nation which it is his high privilege to govern.
I have heard much of a political crisis in recent weeks. There need not be one. I address myself to the Prime Minister through the acting leader of the house: by taking the simple, honest, fearless course he can enlist

Mobilization Act-Mr. Slaght
his critics on his side, and the judgment of history will certainly dissipate any temporary dissension within his party ranks. These tragic days of war will not always be upon us. Surely it is consistent with statesmanship and honour that this nation be governed with a view to the future. I am perfectly conscious that the great job in hand is the effective prosecution of the war, and I am not unmindful of the great contribution this nation has made in many spheres under the present government. But I do feel that when that day arrives when all our sacrifices will be crowned with victory it will be an irreparable tragedy if the British empire's war effort should have suffered because Canada failed to adopt a form of conscription equal to that of the United States. Canada's position geographically makes her the show window of the British commonwealth of nations, influencing American public opinion to a far greater degree than her population of twelve million people would in itself warrant. We cannot afford to prejudice the magnificent contribution of those brave people of England, the senior partner of this commonwealth, by causing a chink in her armour. If the comradeship which is being gained in arms among the Anglo-Saxon nations by the sacrifice of their bravest and best is to bear full fruit in the days of peace, surely it is important that this nation leave no justifiable opportunity for individual patriots in any land to say that Canada among the united nations failed to meet the sacrifices of any other country.
Again I appeal to the Prime Minister to consider our obligations to the future, and to give this house at once a clear-cut measure of conscription, which will enable sacrifices to be equally shared so that the laurels which will accompany victory may be worn with equal pride in every section of this dominion.

speechtext:
Before making some observations on this bill I wish
to compliment the hon. member who has just spoken (Mr. Bruce) on the clearness and tolerance and the excellent manner of delivery of his address. I shall have a word to say a little later as to his introduction into this debate of the name of his honoured leader, but in the meantime I do pay that tribute, a genuine one, to my hon. friend.
Let me say at once that I propose to vote for this bill. Indeed I could find no reason not to do so. I believe I owe it to my constituents and to the people of Canada and to myself to support this bill, in order that the answer given by the people in the plebiscite may have the effect for which they overwhelmingly voted.
What argument can really be found to the contrary? Section 3 of the mobilization act, if it remains the law, is a distinct prohibition against the government introducing compulsory service at such time as they may in the light of all the circumstances of the moment deem it essential so to do in order to maintain Canada's war effort. Therefore I find no difficulty whatever in believing that it is my bounden duty to vote for Bill No. 80.
How can we justify any other course? If occasion arises, if our voluntary system should fail-the contrary is the fact for the moment -the government should, I believe, be free to act speedily and fearlessly by introducing a measure to provide for compulsory service, in order that we may at all times reinforce and support and not desert the young men of this country whom we have sent overseas, whom we have voted money to support, whom we are maintaining, French-Canadian and English, in Britain and elsewhere to fight Canada's battle over there.
I feel that some confusion has crept into this debate because we have not realized the importance of one of the main factors, and I should like to put it to hon. members now. Canada has a budget, or if you like a programme, under which to carry on the war.
We budgeted wisely in advance, not merely for money-we had our money budget on Tuesday and that will be discussed at the proper time-but for our man-power needs in all three armed forces, as all nations do. We budgeted for the fifteen-months period for our man-power requirements, from January 1, 1942, to March 31, 1943; we announced the budget to parliament and received the assent of parliament, practically unanimously, to our man-power budget. Our war cabinet did not do that lightly. You heard from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) that he had consulted the high commands of all our Canadian forces. Next they consulted and received the approval of our much
Mobilization Act-Mr. Slaght

respected and revered chief of the armed forces, General McNaughton, who also approved our man-power budget. Next, as the minister has told you, he secured the approval, although it was not necessary at all to do so, of the British Secretary of State for War to the sufficiency and propriety of our budget.
We budgeted to increase our forces-the members are all familiar with the details- from 27,000 men now in the navy to 40,000 by March of next year. We need 80,000 more young men in. the air force to bring the strength up from 100,000 to 180,000, and we need from 90,000 to 100,000 more men in the army to bring it up to the requirements of the two army corps set out in the manner indicated by the minister, it is on Hansard, and I shall not repeat it. So that the total budget of our man-power by March next is
615,000	men for all the armed forces. I have heard no man in this house or out of it declare that he has any quarrel with those figures or with that objective, with that budget or with that programme. If there is any such, let him indicate to me now that he does not think it is enough, having regard to those who approved this budget, and having regard to the well-known fact that generals as a rule want all the men they can get. With General McNaughton's approval of that budget, I have not heard a man in Canada, not even a newspaper in Canada, say that it was not an ample and proper budget, when you remember what we have to do in the other fields of total war effort.
Those other fields I shall not dwell on, but there is the food supply. We supply from Canada to-day two-thirds of the food of the British isles. We are supplying now three times more food to Britain every month than we supplied during the corresponding period of the whole course of the last war. We have also greatly increased our munitions supply, our supply of automotive vehicles, and of all that comes under the head of munitions. W7e are supplying eight times more munitions for the allies now than we did at any time in the last war. Remember those two facts, and do not let us get out of gear when we attempt to determine whether Canada's war effort is one of which we may be proud, and not one, as I am afraid some hon. members have almost indicated, at which we must hang our heads for fear the United States might laugh at us or sneer at us because our war effort was insufficient. I do not believe that the great majority of the decent people of the United States have any such notion in their hearts or heads at all. Would we be a proper subject for their laughter or 
their sneers when by a purely voluntary effort, without the least compulsion, we have done everything the mother country has asked us to do, and when, in the midst of this budget period, we are over-subscribed in money and in men for all three armed forces? And Canada is doing all that on a voluntary basis!
May I digress for a moment, Mr. Speaker, to deal with an incidental topic which I am sure you will feel is in order but which nevertheless is a little off my thesis. The United States recently raised the minimum monthly pay of any soldier in the United States army to 850 a month. After listening to the budget delivered in this house two days ago I say that we in this country ought at once to put similar legislation on our statute books. The soldiers of that great country and our own have almost everything in common-their mode of living, their scale of subsistence, their common desires, their common expenditures. All these things make them practically parallel, and I do not want to feel that these boys of ours, when they get over there, will be fighting shoulder to shoulder in a great crisis yet to come with the gallant troops from the United States and be receiving only $39 a month while the soldiers of the United States receive S50. I believe that we can afford to pay them $50, and we ought to do it. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) touched on this subject the other day, and I am heartily in agreement with him. He deserves great credit for bringing it to our attention.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Would the hon. member elaborate for a moment on the dependents' allowance, which makes, I think, a little difference?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
My hon. friend is correct. But dependents' allowance or no dependents' allowance-and what we are paying is not any too much for those dependents

we should raise the soldiers pay to $50 a month as a minimum. If the Minister of Finance has any doubts about it, then the least he should do, although I would prefer that he pay the $50 to them now every month, would be t6 let the difference between $39 and $50 accumulate as savings for the soldier, to be paid to him at the end of the war.
I have a word to say to two types of people on the subject of this debate. They are very different types. The first type is the man from Quebec or anywhere else in Canada, whether in or out of this house-and there are very few in this house to whom my remarks will apply at all-who says: I am against any young man from Canada going out of Canada

to fight. Unfortunately there are some few people in this country to-day who take that position, who say: I will not send any Canadian boy or be a party to sending him outside Canada to war anywhere, at any time, under any circumstances. I am referring now to the absolute isolationist, who says that under no method, voluntary or compulsory, will he be a party to a boy from Canada fighting outside of Canada. That is the old Duplessis doctrine which we fought to a standstill a couple of years ago, when the gallant people of Quebec, to their credit-I had no part in the contest-indicated decisively that they would have no part in that doctrine in this war.
Why did Canada declare war on Germany? When we came here in September 1939 did we put a mushy declaration on the statute book that if Germany came over here we would get out our g ns and fight her? No; Canada declared war on Germany, and Canada said, "We will stand beside the mother country, and we will help her whip Germany to her knees." That in effect was the declaration of war, if hon. members will look it up and read it, as I did this morning. And what else could you expect, in declaring war, than to proceed to send men to fight the enemy outside of Canada, wherever the enemy could be found?
Do you people who say we should not send men out of Canada to fight expect some day to whip Germany in Canada? Is that the theory on which we .declared war-to whip Germany in Canada? To ask the question is to answer it. I say to my hon. friends from Quebec-to the very few I am now addressing -you joined gallantly with us in September, 1939 in declaring war on Germany. You joined with us for three years in voting moneys-to do what? To send overseas our armed forces who enlisted voluntarily. You joined with us in Red Cross activities-not to have bandages waiting down in Quebec, but to send bandages to meet all needs and mercies to the Red Cross overseas. Those bandages were to follow our men, to be ready if disaster should come.
You have also followed us in respect to our air force. Could it be said by the isolationist that he intended only that our airmen should fly up and down over Manitoba and Quebec? Was it intended that they should not go outside the country? What arrant nonsense that would be I We created an air force-the greatest thing Canada has ever done since confederation-which has attracted the eyes of the w'hole world. We created that air force to go over there and fight the enemy where they can find him.
Mobilization Act-Mr. Slaght
We created the air force to whip him in Germany and to fight in Germany-and that is what they are doing.
All over the world our boys are to be found-and 1 shall not give the details, because they were put on Hansard the other day.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: To China.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Yes, even to China. And
what about the navy? Did we build up that gallant navy in order that they might sail up and down lake Erie, or up and down lake Ontario, or perhaps even down the St. Lawrence river-"but if they get eleven miles out, don't dare let the boys go outside the twelve-mile limit"! What arrant nonsense, again! We created a navy in order that it might brave the perils of the Atlantic to meet the enemy, and we have been doing it, ever since the war started, in the finest and most splendid way. Let us, therefore, have a truce to all these suggestions that the boys should not be sent outside of Canada to fight for Canada and whip Germany, to win the war.
That is the first type of person to which I wished to direct my first observations. The second type of person is the man who says, "Enforce conscription right away. Put it on the books to-morrow. Don't wait another moment." There are some hon. members to whom I wish to pay the greatest credit, because I am of the opinion that they believe that to be the best thing to do. But will they permit me to examine for a moment whether or not we should take that course, having in mind the plight in which we find ourselves on this 25th day of June, 1942.
Let me refer to the observations made yesterday by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White), speaking to this bill. He asked that on the third reading- and I trust I may refer to my notes in this connection-the government should introduce all necessary rules and regulations to make conscription enforcible, and that we should go on and debate all the petty details, every little item, and sit here I suppose all summer, or possibly into the fall-perhaps even up to Christmastide. Meantime Hitler and the Japanese would not be waiting for us. I entirely disagree with the hon. member's suggestion that the house should follow details of that kind. It may be that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) would agree with him.	[DOT]
Let me for the benefit of the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough look a little deeper into his suggestion. It is important to recall that in 1917 a conscription bill was placed upon the statute book, and assent was given to

Mobilization Act-Mr. Slaght

that bill on August 29 of that year. There was provision that the measure should become effective on December 1, 1917. It was introduced by a Unionist government, containing within its ranks splendid Canadians of both stripes of politics, Canadian from both the great political parties. Our new-found friends to the left had hardly come out of their swaddling clothes, or perhaps were not even born at that time-and I make that observation in no offensive way.
I call attention to the fact that in 1917 the government headed by Sir Robert Borden joined with eminent Canadian Liberals such as the late revered Mr. Rowell-I shall not name them, because history has recorded their names-and that government went to the country on the question of conscription. On December 19, having brought in a bill and having wrestled with it in parliament, as my hon. friend would have us do now-the hon. member from the west will recall the occasion-and having settled all the details with respect to it, the people of Canada passed upon it, and declared overwhelmingly in favour of conscription, on a vote of 153 for and 82 against.
In promoting that legislation Sir Robert Borden said to the people of Canada earlier in the year, back in May or June, ''We must have 70,000 more men by December 31." That was one of his great pleas. That was the only way he could get them. What happened? When December 31 came they did not have even 7.000 more men. January, February and March passed by, and they had called up
404,000	men all across Canada, under conscription. It is recorded that 380,000 applications for exemptions had been filed. Of the total registrants called up, the proportion from Ontario was 125,000.
In order to have my figures accurate perhaps at this stage I could not do better than to read an extract from a most revered author who has now passed away. I refer to the late Doctor O. D. Skelton, a man who for fifteen years under different governments was Undersecretary of State for External Affairs, and a man who was held in the highest respect, as was so clearly indicated on the occasion of his passing in July of last year. As an historian of integrity he has had something to say about conscription, an issue which it was his duty to follow very closely. I quote the following from page 545, volume 2, as filed in the parliamentary library:
It failed absolutely-
He was referring to conscription.
-in the ostensible aim of providing greater reinforcements than the voluntary system. The government had had a free hand in framing [Mr. Slaght.1
the measure. No effort or expense was spared in its enforcement. A huge administrative staff was set up, each office with its full equipment of shining desks and elaborate files; forms and instructions and regulations rained from the printing bureau; medical officers and reviewing boards, local tribunals, appeal courts and a central appeal judge (Mr. Justice Duff) were appointed, with militia representatives to check exemptions; police were enrolled to round up defaulters. In Quebec as elsewhere, once the issue was decided at the polls, the act was accepted, and its operation given full scope. Yet the legions promised did not appear. The first shock to the sanguine supporters of the act came when it was found that of the 404,000 of the first class, unmarried men from twenty' to thirty-four, who had registered by the end of 1917, 380,000 had claimed exemption; the next, with the announcement that there were
118.000	claims for exemption from Ontario as against 115,000 from Quebec (out of 125,000 and 117,000 registrants).
Will the hon. member for Parlcdale digest that little morsel?

The lost leader.

speechtext: Not bad.
