speechtext:
Not bad, but is my hon. friend saying that the discrepancy between the figures for Ontario and Quebec justifies the language we heard yesterday across the floor of this house? No. I continue with Doctor Skelton:
Local tribunals, particularly in Quebec, were charged with being farcically lax; on the other hand, the military representatives appealed nearly every exemption in Quebec, but allowed
90.000	in Ontario to go unopposed. Exemptions were reviewed by the appeal judges and later by Justice Duff: by the end of March, some
364.000	out of 372,000 cases had been decided.
In Quebec 108,000 exemptions had been finally approved, and in Ontario 104,000. Sir Robert Borden had insisted in June inat :t was absolutely essential to have 70,000 men by December 31, 1917. By March 31	1918, the number
ordered to report for duty was on'y 31,000, of whom 5.000 defaulted, the net yield being less than 26,000. Supporters of conscription were slow to admit its failure, 1 -t in the face of this breakdown criticism could not wholly be suppressed.
Then there is a quotation from the Montreal Gazette. I think this is one of the newspapers loudest in support of conscription. It was not playing politics when it said:
The spectacle offered by the operation of the draft system has not been encouraging. The government appears to have established a system which if it gets the men at all, will get them so slowly that whatever military advantage depends upon expeditious reinforcement will be lost.
I am sorry the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) is not here, for thr Toronto Globe referred to the widespread feeling of disappointment, while it is said that Mayor Church of Toronto stated:
The Military Service Act will cost the country millions and is getting very little results. If 44561-2345
the government had spent one-quarter of the money in voluntary recruiting, they would have got more men.
I am not quoting this to annoy my hon. friend from Toronto. I believe he is as loyal a man as there is in this house. If I may say so, I think he has been rather misled by his absentee leader.
I have just a few more quotations from Doctor Skelton's book. This gives the worst side of the picture. I want to be fair, because there is another item. I quote from page 548 as follows:
The military crisis caused by the German drive for the channel ports in March gave occasion for a change in policy. The government decided to cancel all exemptions granted to men of twenty, twenty-one and twenty-two years of age. A resolution sanctioning an order in council to this effect passed parliament by a vote of 114 to 65.
The matter was carefully reviewed in parliament, and this order called up men who were entitled to stay home. Parliament did that, and parliament had the right to do it. Doctor Skelton continues:
When the end came in November, 1918, some
83.000	men had been enrolled under the act, or had reported voluntarily after its enactment; of these, 7,000 were on compassionate leave and
15.000	on farm leave, so that the actual yield was 61,000 men, of whom few ever saw France.
What does that mean? We were to have
70.000	men by the end of December, 1917, but at the end of March, 1918, we had only 26.000. While the figures show that 61.000 were obtained as a result of that compulsion during the whole period up to armistice day, November 11, during the same period 101,000 men enlisted voluntarily.
I suggest that our fight must go on. A man who talks of peace now ought to be stuck up against a wall and shot. It would be nothing but a German peace; we would be putting our people into slavery for the rest of their existence. To my friends from Quebec, for many of whom I have the highest personal regard, let me say this in the friendliest spirit. The one sure way to avoid conscription for overseas is to continue the good work that you are doing of voluntary enlistments in ever-increasing numbers. That is the solution. Let all our provinces unite in friendly competition to supply men for the armed forces in this great struggle.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext: Like Prince Edward Island.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Like little Prince Edward Island. We shall have a hard time, in any province, to beat their record.
I have referred, perhaps insufficiently, to the fact that Quebec has done well in the armed forces under the voluntary system.
Mobilization Act-Mr. Slaght

Thousands and thousands of our best boys in the navy, guarding and convoying and doing all the dirty work of the seas, come from Quebec, and you may be proud of them. Thousands and thousands of the young men in our air force-those who are over the channel, over Great Britain, over Germany-come from your province, and you may be proud of them. I had the privilege some ten days ago of attending a function, just outside these noble buildings, when two young French Canadians, Robillard and Morin, were acclaimed by a multitude of
20,000	people. French Canadians came in thousands from the other side of the river and we English-speaking people joined with them in a tribute to these two young heroes. They did not spend their time in the air over Manitoba or Quebec; they were over Germany, and we should not overlook the fact that the youth of Quebec turned out on that occasion with us and paid the greatest tribute to boys who were willing to go and did go and fight overseas, and were decorated by His Majesty the King. Let us keep up the tradition those two lads have set for the province of Quebec.
I conclude with this suggestion. Let us live our Canada as we believe she should be lived. Let us ban all those sayings which come so readily to the lips, and set race against race. Let us understand that we have had a wonderful history and record as a nation under the most difficult circumstances. Let us not forget those wonderful words which Winston Churchill uttered more than a year ago, and which apply with even greater force to-day: "There is grave reason for vigilance and concern, but no room for despair." I say to you, my fellow Canadians of the House of Commons and any across Canada who may hear or learn of what I have said: Let us join together in unity. The danger is terrific. What might happen is unthinkable unless we make a common cause, unless we show a common front, unless we go out to stop the enemy from destroying the motherland. Were the British fleet to go-I am not uttering these reflections as a harbinger of evil, but we must think of what might happen-how long would it be before the enemy's ships and their dastardly agents of destruction would be up the St. Lawrence river, through the fair province of Quebec, desecrating your cathedrals, blasting your schools, ravishing your loved ones? I say to my hon. friends across the way, as well as those by my side: Can any of us afford to do anything but adopt a course which is all for the greatness and glory of Canada? Let
[Mr. Slaght.l
us not forget that little sentence which I like so much: "There is always a far horizon for forward-looking men."

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words on this allimportant resolution, but I experience some timidity in speaking after the eloquent member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght) who has just resumed his seat.
I think it is my duty to say a few words on this matter on behalf of my riding and the good electors whom I represent. Much has been said in this house; many speeches have been made-many of them read. Mine has not been written: I shall just utter a few expressions on this important subject.
I consider it a great honour to represent the constituency of Nipissing, which extends, on the direct line from east to west, stretching from the Ottawa river to Georgian bay, a distance of two hundred miles, and another two hundred miles from north to south. In the election of 1935 there were nearly 63.000 voters on the lists, and without boasting I may say that I held eighty-six meetings during the campaign. In other words, to be the member for Nipissing is a full-time job. The riding is composed partly of rural and partly of urban people. We have a nice farming country; we have also the cities of North Bay and Sudbury, containing populations of 17,000 and 34,000 respectively. Of my electors, about 40 per cent are of Anglo-Saxon origin, about 40 per cent French, and the remainder of other nationalities.
Since this war began I hav" been astonished to see the patriotism, good-will and generosity of all those citizens, regardless of race, creed or politics. It would have been the wish of the people of North Bay and Sudbury to have separate regiments of their own, as they had in the last war, which did such marvellous deeds then, but we were told by the military authorities that this was not possible in view of the fact that uniformity in training was highly desirable. We therefore accepted their decision. Nevertheless, in the constituency of Nipissing our citizens have enlisted by thousands from the very start, and regardless of race or religion they have come forward- English, Scotch, Irish, French, Italian, Greek, Finns, Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Serbs, Croatians and Indians. Some of them have ' joined Scottish regiments, the Royal Engineers, the Grey and Simcoe, the 14th Forestry Tank Corps and many other units. In the first Scottish regiment that was recruited, there are to be seen, I am proud to say, men of many nationalities wearing the kilts. They have continued to enlist in this way until the present

Mobilization Act-Mr. Hurtubise
day. Every time the military authorities have asked for a quota in my district the best young men have come forward. There has been complete cooperation on the part of everyone. Our citizens have accepted the situation with patriotism and generosity. They have been willing to bear the restrictions that have been imposed from time to time. They have willingly paid their taxes and have made various contributions to the war effort. We have played our part. All our public bodies have cooperated. I might cite one example of generosity and patriotism. At the time of military registration in North Bay, that city did all the work gratuitously. I do not know that this was done in many other places, but it shows the spirit of the people in that part of my riding.
In 1930 the electors of Nipissing did me the honour of returning me to represent them at Ottawa. I am not so credulous as to suppose that they voted mainly for myself. They voted for the party led by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and for those supporting him. Since that time they have voted for the same party as a government, and they have done so with increasing majorities. Again, I do not take credit for this; I give it to the Prime Minister and his government. In 1930 the majority in my district for the government party was 2.000; in 1935, 12,000, and in 1940, almost 16,000.
In the plebiscite, those who voted in my constituency returned 4,868 of a majority in favour of the affirmative. Many things have been said about the plebiscite, and I have taken the trouble to go around my constituency in order to find out the sentiments of the people. I want to be perfectly frank with the members of this house as well as with my electors. I admit that many voted "yes", for conscription, while many voted against conscription; but a great mass of the people voted neither for nor against conscription but simply as a means of expressing confidence in the present administration and so giving directions for a continuance of the present war effort. They voted to release the government from its past commitments. That was the attitude of a great part of the voters in my county, and I am sure that if a straight vote had been taken for or against conscription the result would have been different.
The question of conscription has been brought up in different campaigns that have been held in my district. It was discussed during the plebiscite, and it has been the chief topic of discussion during this debate. Widely different opinions have been expressed, but the conclusion I have drawn from the
discussion, from all the speeches and the different statements that have been made, is that there is no great necessity for the immediate imposition of conscription. Why should there be pressure for the immediate imposition of conscription when we had the experience, as stated a few moments ago by the member for Parry Sound, which we had in the last war, when the results that w'ere obtained were so unsatisfactory. It proved altogether impracticable. Judged by the results, the method was then a failure.
Since this question first came up we have-had statements in the house from the different war ministers indicating that until now we have filled all our quotas; that, indeed, we have been in advance of our quotas, in regard to the army, the navy and the air force. The various ministers have proved this beyond any doubt. We have complied with the demands of our own military authorities and with the demands of the combined allied military authorities. Mr. Churchill made the statement that our contribution to the war effort was magnificent, and yet in spite of that we have heard a good many speeches-and violent speeches at that-in favour of conscription. I cannot understand it. For some days now we have been hearing from different ministers that for the present there is no necessity for conscription. I believe that Canadians are generous enough, loyal enough, to continue to answer the call in numbers great enough to fill the needs, and this voluntarily. But no one knows when the war will end or what the necessities for Canada or for the rest of the world will be in the future. However, I have confidence in the Prime Minister and in his cabinet, and I believe that they will act wisely under the circumstances that exist at any time. That is why I intend to support the present resolution, because I have full confidence in the government. I know they will not act unwisely. I know they will bear in mind always, as they have done from the beginning, that a total war effort means a well-balanced war effort. They know that if they should throw this total war effort out of balance! it would be disastrous for Canada and would greatly impair our contribution in this war.
The question of conscription has given rise to a great deal of discussion against my compatriots. I am a French-Canadian anc I am proud of the fact. Although my father and mother were born in Quebec, I was bon in Ontario and I was brought up and educated in that province, except for my arts course. I have lived in contact with the English speaking people of my part of the country- I might say mainly with the Scotch people-
3698	COMMONS
Mobilization Act-Mr. Hurtubise
I have got to know them, and I think we have always co-operated well together. With good-will we can go very far. Yes; I was brought up among Scotch people. I remember very well that my mother could understand English but could not speak it, and our neighbour-Martha Campbell-was a good old lady who cound understand French but could not speak it. They were, however, great friends and used to visit each other and have long conversations together, one speaking in English and the other in French, and they understood each other very well. That shows that with good-will we can always work together in a friendly spirit.
After my university course in the good Scotch Presbyterian university of Queens I went north to what I think is the most cosmopolitan part of the whole of Canada; it is about 40 per cent British stock, 40 per cent French and the remaining 20 per cent of various racial origins. Yet I may say we have always agreed together very well. I have been there for about thirty-five years; I grew up with our chief towns and cities, and I know the mentality of the people. We agree together very well although we differ in race and religion. I remember that before the last war there was some antipathy between different groups-and let me say I believe that such antipathy between people of different race or religion is always due to ignorance, lack of contact, nothing else. I have seen proof of it. In my own constituency before the last war there were groups that looked upon one another with some antagonism, but the contacts made during the last war between men of different races and religions did great good in bringing those men together and creating a real national ideal and unity. I know men of both races who went to the last war very narrow-minded and who came back real Canadians ready to cooperate in a fraternal spirit with their fellow citizens.
The question of conscription, which has been talked of so much in this debate, has been approached from a very bad angle, mainly, I would say, by the extremists. If we are broad enough to take the people as they are and treat them as they are, we shall have greater cooperation and less friction. Those who understand the French Canadians and have the right approach to them have always found 100 per cent cooperation. I want to cite one great Canadian who sat in the seat now occupied by the hon. member for Parkdale.
I refer to Mr. C. H. Cahan of Montreal. I think he was one of the greatest of Canadians; he was Canadian first and all the time. This is what he had to say in March, 1939, speaking 
of foreign policy, as reported at page 2497 of Hansard of that year. I think it covers the subject very well as far as the mentality of the French Canadians in the last war and the reason for that mentality are concerned. He said:
Therefore as far as I am concerned I stand by and support the attitude taken this afternoon by the Minister of Justice.
That was the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. Mr. Cahan continued:
I could go on and say many things in support of his suggestion that at the time of the outbreak of the last war the province of Quebec and the people of the French-Canadian race were placed in a very difficult position indeed. But I could write a volume to show, I think, that the great body of sentiment in that province was in favour of cooperation; but it resisted coercion at a time when coercion was not necessary.
As was proven by the hon. member for Parry Sound a few minutes ago. A little further on Mr. Cahan said, as reported at page 2498 of the same Hansard:
That, after all, is the spirit of the French people; but you must treat them with the consideration, respect and esteem which they deserve and which we often fail to give. If that is done, and it comes to another great conflict, if it comes under this government I am sure other methods, more conciliatory, will be followed; and if they are followed you will find the young men of the French Canadian race-I know them better in the country districts, perhaps, than in the cities-ready and anxious to play their part and do their share of service alongside their Canadian fellow subjects. Coersion will not be necessary in Quebec if you exercise conciliation and respect the mentality and traditions of the great people who founded that race, particularly-and I hope this will not be offensive to any person-those of the Norman race to which so many of us actually belong. I can make that statement with some pride, because my grandmother on one side came from the Huguenots and had strong French sympathies.
This great decision, if it has to be made, may have to be made suddenly. If so, the whole matter of Canada's active participation in war must be decided by the Canadian parliament, and, through parliament, by the Canadian people. But if that issue is raised, if my fellow Canadians in the province of Quebec realize that the question of neutrality involves the severance of Canada from the British empire and from the British crown, I have no doubt as to the decision that the thoughtful people will make.
I sometimes talk to the leading clergy of Quebec and to those men who lead public opinion on various sides of politics in Quebec, and I am persuaded that the thoughtful and intelligent men of that province believe that the preservation of those religious and racial rights which they hold sacred depends upon Canada remaining a part of the British empire, because in no other state in Europe or in America is there the same freedom of religious opinion and of religious worship as is to be found throughout the British empire under the crown.

Mobilization Act-Mr. Howden
I heard those words across the floor of this house in 1939. Mr. Cahan, I think, knows the people of Quebec province as well as anyone. I have known Mr. Cahan by reputation for many years; I have followed his writings in books and papers, and have always thought he was a great Canadian; and I think his opinion on this subject should be worth something.
He said that the question of conscription should be decided by parliament. That is something I was always led to believe. I have confidence in my leader and his cabinet, but we have a right to our personal opinions and I may disagree on some points. I say here and now that I regret very much that this question is not directly submitted to parliament for decision. That is what we were promised in the past. Still I have enough confidence in the present prime minister and his cabinet to do the wisest thing under the circumstances, for the reasons I stated a few minutes ago.
Some might think that as a French Canadian I have spoken in a queer manner on the racial question. But I was brought up under different circumstances and had the opportunity of seeing both sides. There is not very much difference between French Canadians, and when I say that I really mean those of Norman descent-and, let us say, the Orangemen of Ontario. The difficulty is that we do not know each other. Anybody who has read history knows that the Normans were descendants of the Norwegians, of the Norsemen. In the revolution under the Vikings, those who were defeated emigrated to the south shore of the English channel and some to the east coast of England. Later the Norman kings conquered England. They were people of French education; they gave to England Magna Charts and its form of government, and there in England they found their brothers on the east coast who had left Norway many years before. We French Canadians of Norman descent have been separated from France for a long time. France in the meantime was progressing through an evolution, and England came over and took possession of Canada and implanted here British institutions. We French Canadians have adopted those British institutions and have learned to love and cherish them and to defend them. Yes; we are lovers of British institutions, though probably the great majority of French Canadians do not know why. It is because we have found in those British institutions the ideals of our forefathers, who themselves were lovers of liberty. That is why I cited this afternoon the words of Mr. Cahan, when he spoke of
coercion versus cooperation. With our mentality, French Canadians are lovers of liberty and freedom; we do not like coercion, and it will be hard ever to make French Canadians swallow it. If, however, they are approached in the proper way, they will be found just as loyal to Canada and to our king as anybody else. But they will not stand coercion. With the proper approach you will find among the French Canadians as much cooperation and enlistment and fighting for king and country as among any other Canadians.
I had no speech prepared, Mr. Speaker, and have made these few remarks because I thought I might help in these difficult times to bring us closer together. Every individual, every nation has made mistakes in the past. Why spend this precious time in mutual reproaches. Let us forget our little difficulties, our little racial and political animosities because, after all, we have all the same ideals, the same ambition and the same end in view-to win this war. So let us put aside this little political fight that has been going on. I think the time has come when we should cut short all this discussion and give a free hand to the government by passing this bill. Let ils members of parliament show our confidence in the government as the people of Canada showed their confidence in the government in March. I for one am sure that the government will do the right thing at the right time, and without throwing out of balance our present war effort.

The young go forth to lay their lives on the altar of patriotism.
The other night I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Quebec West and South (Mr. Parent), one which was most excellent and full of force and eloquence. He indicated that his compatriots from Quebec were willing, if necessary, to give their lives for this Canadian country, as it stretches from the green meadows of Prince Edward Island to the pine-clad mountains on the Pacific coast. But he pointed out that when Canada was ceded to Great Britain, French Canadians had been given assurances that they would not be asked to fight outside this country for Britain, and that they w'ould never agree willingly to do so.
As he spoke I felt sympathetically toward him. In my opinion much of what he said was true, and I thought at the time that I should like to vote as he will vote. But at the same time I had a vision of a man who lived in a house in a city. One night he heard the sound of running feet, and cries of "fire". After a time he noticed that the confusion appeared to concentrate round his own house, and there appeared to be loud and excited conversation. Hearing this, he went to the window and saw a great throng of people talking excitedly. Looking round, he observed that his neighbour's house, not many feet from his, was on fire. But he said to himself, "Oh, well, it is not my house; I do not need to be particularly concerned; I shall just go back to bed and settle down." Then,

after a time there was a knock on his door, and someone said, "Do you know the house next door is on fire, and the wind is blowing in your direction?" But his reply was, "Oh, that is all right; I need not worry about that; it is not my house." He retired again. After another short time there was a loud banging at his door, and the people said, "Do you know your house is on fire?" Then, indeed, did he bestir himself. Then, indeed, did he dress in a hurry, get his family out, and do what he could to save his possessions. But it was too late; his house was burning.
It occurred to me that that was about the position in which many people from French Canada are placing themselves to-day. They are not willing to get out and bestir themselves when the houses just opposite are burning. They seem prepared to wait until their own house is in flames. What chance will there be if the people of Canada wait until the invader is at our doors?-and he is at our doors. If they wait until the invader is at our doors, what hope is there? There is none whatsoever.
The issue under debate is plain enough. I need not refer again to the various elements which enter into the discussion. I might say briefly, however, that on the one hand there are many strong elements of British extraction who demand immediate conscription. On the other hand we have many French Canadians- not all of them, it is true-who steadfastly resist the application of that principle. I would preface my further remarks by asking two questions which seem to bear on this subject. First, why are the French Canadians so bitterly opposed to conscription? Second, why are other people so determined to have immediate conscription?
Let us turn to the first question, as to why the French Canadians are so bitterly opposed, and consider the corollary as to why Quebec and French Canadians should require pledges, more than others. In that connection I would refer to the remarks of the former Minister of Transport and Public Works (Mr. Cardin) who, in his observations, sought to explain the first question in these words:
But when we come to consider problems such as the one confronting us at the present time, immediately any man who has any elementary knowledge of psychology will understand that your response is going to be much quicker than mine. Why? Because I have to reason in my mind why I have to support the British flag and spend my energies for the defence of British race in this conflict, or perhaps elsewhere. It is the result of thinking, the result of reasoning, if I come to that conclusion; with you it is the impulse of the heart. Your heart becomes inflamed as soon as the name of England, of the British empire, is mentioned.

hundred years ago, history records. Their tradition is French; their language is French; their education and their religion are of the French Catholic church.

Not only that, but I believe they were very much better used by their new English masters than they had been by many of their French governors. They were satisfied, and they played the game with Great Britain as is shown by their actions at the time of the revolt of the United States, in 1775, and again in 1849. For the next hundred years after the conquest of Canada the French Canadians were well satisfied.
The patriotic zeal of the French Canadian swung away from old France at the time of the revolution when that country forsook royalty and religion. However, when the patriotic regard of the French Canadian for old France was withdrawn, it was not turned to Great Britain by any means. At this time the people of Quebec transferred their allegiance from the fatherland in Europe to their own home in Canada. Canada became their new country. Canada was their only country. They owed allegiance to no other land than Canada. I may be wrong, but it is my opinion that with all the respect and loyalty that remained in the hearts of the French-Canadian people, with regard to the British empire, there was never any indication of filial love for the great empire. So long as the people of French Canada were not asked to take part in British wars which might take them out of the country, everything was all right; everything was quiet. This afternoon we have heard of the great number of young French Canadians who have enlisted voluntarily in this war, as well as of those who enlisted voluntarily in the last war. However, on every occasion when there was any suggestion of coercion or compulsion or
domination, the French, who are a fiery, sensitive and proud people, resented it and fought against it as they are fighting to-day.
The hon. member for Riehelieu-Vereheres was only half right. He referred to the Canadian people who were burning with patriotic fire. I should like to point out the difference between the French people with their French traditions and those of British origin. I never learned it at school, and I certainly never learned it at church, but I always thought of Canada as being a member of a great British family. I thought of Canada as being a family herself and as being one of many other families. When any one of those families got into trouble their relatives and their friends came to their assistance. I well remember 1884, when I was not a very big boy, when the young men of Winnipeg went on the Nile voyage to the siege of Khartum. That is my earliest international memory. Then the next year we had the northwest rebellion, and I remember the redcoats from Toronto in the old Canadian Pacific Railway depot who had come out to help our 90th battalion, the so-called Little Black Devils. That seemed only natural to me.
When I first heard it said that the sun never set on the British empire I thrilled with pride. I have always had that feeling about Canada and about Great Britain. After all, we are one of a great conglomeration of people with like sympathies and a like purpose in life. This seems to me to be perhaps the most outstanding difference between us of British origin and those of French origin. The latter came from France, and they had a filial connection with that country which they threw off after the conquest of Canada. On the other hand, we are of British extraction. I am the fourth generation of my family in this country, but I am afraid that I have never been consumed with this so-called patriotic fire. At any time that the British empire has become involved in trouble I have felt a decided sense of duty and obligation, but it has been a well considered idea.

The reason why the French detest conscription dates back, of course, to the conquest of Canada. No one likes the humility of defeat, and the French are a proud and sensitive people. For nearly two hundred years they owned this land, which had been, in the words of of the former Minister of Transport and public works (Mr. Cardin), wrested from the wilderness and the savages and given to Christianity by their forefathers. Through the early terrible years they suffered many hardships and privations. They defended the land against raiding Indians and against the invasion of the English colonists. Often their early settlements were wiped out with fire and massacre. But they persisted; they held on. They turned forests into farms; they built roads, villages, communities and fortified cities. After two hundred years their land was handed over by the crown of France to that of Great Britain. Fortunately, their new masters were, comparatively speaking, easy and much less offensive than some of their rulers from the old land.
Now, sir, at confederation the people of French Canada received, in my opinion, a very satisfactory arrangement. About a hundred years passed, during which they were quite satisfied and contented; they had very little to complain of; but when, in 1885, when Riel was hanged, Quebec was not so happy. Riel was a French Catholic. He was a dreamer, an impractical dreamer, who had visions of setting up an independent republic in Rupert's Land, with himself as president and the local archbishop enthroned as the pontiff. That may sound ridiculous, but that is the fact.

Quebec looked upon the whole western move as an extension of empire, and many felt that Riel had come to an untimely and unjust end. Probably that is the first incident in the history of Canada since confederation that estranged the people of Quebec to some extent.
At the time of the South African war Quebec looked with disfavour upon the sending of Canadians to assist Britain. We remember that the British interests were roughly discriminated against in the South African Dutch republic and that the Jameson raid was in the form of a rebellious protest; but it is questionable if it justified the government of Britain in later attacking that republic and subjecting it to British rule. In any event, it was the beginning of the French-Canadian nationalist movement which was in protest, first of all, against the extension of British imperialism and also against Canadians being called upon to fight Britain's imperialistic wars overseas.
The next trouble came during the great war. It was well known by this time that the people of Quebec, while prepared to fight and die in the defence of Canada, had no sympathy whatever for British imperialism and disavowed any responsibility or obligation in relation thereto. When, therefore, Russia backed Serbia, France backed Russia and England backed France against Germany and Hungary in 1914, it certainly looked like a war of conquest for national aggrandizement. When a bill for conscription was brought into this house in 1917 by a union government preponderantly British, and a union government preponderantly British was used to push it through, Quebec opposed it fiercely and sent a solid phalanx to oppose it. Quebec took the attitude that we were in reality an independent nation, that there was no obligation to send men overseas, and fiercely resented compulsion in the matter of securing men for the army. I am disposed to think that the people of Quebec were not far wrong, particularly when defeat in the last war could not likely have made so much difference to Canada, and when one feels that the union government had more fish to fry than one, and that besides the provision of men for the army there was the little matter of the Canadian National and Grand Trunk investments to be considered.
At the outbreak of the present war no political party in Canada felt that conscription was necessary or that there was any need indeed for sending men overseas, and they so stated in this house and out of it. Pledges were given to Canadians everywhere that there would certainly be no conscription for
overseas, and when this pledge was challenged by the Premier of Quebec we all know what happened. Small wonder then that when the government sought release from this pledge and used the preponderance of the British vote by way of the plebiscite to overrule the French, and when now this government seeks to remove the last barrier, the French people feel that they have been betrayed and look with distrust on the action of the government.
I would now turn to question number 2 and ask why other Canadians, as typified largely by members of the official opposition, are so set on immediate conscription for men overseas, when there is at present no apparent need. That there has been a well sustained effort in this house and out of it by members of the opposition and their friends to force the government to apply conscription will hardly be denied. Then, conscious of the well-known aversion of French Canadians, and of the fact that with two exceptions the French Canadian group in this house are supporters of the Liberal government, and the further fact that the application of conscription will probably-at any rate possibly if not probably-bring about national disunity, why do the members of the opposition insist on a measure of this kind? Do they seek to create a cleavage in party support in the chamber?

Mr. NORMAN J. M. LOCKHART (Lincoln): I shall humbly bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and endeavour to the best of my ability not even to refer to my notes, any more than I can possibly help.
At the outset of my remarks I wish to refer to the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) who, when giving, during this debate, his review of the accomplishments of his department, gave us a very clear description of what had been done, for which I think he deserves a great deal of credit, in giving leadership to such an accomplishment as has been developed by the industrial forces of this country. I am sure the minister knows that I have no animosity toward him and will do anything I can to help him; but I must say this, that not many months ago an urgent demand was made to members of this house -it was to myself and, I know, to other members with whom I have conferred-urging that industrialists and the great army of industrial workers be given an opportunity to make tanks and aeroplanes in Canada. The minister, improperly advised I think, said that this was impossible on account of lack of technical men and for other reasons which were stated. I know that answer did not please the great body of industrial men in this country; it did not suit the army of industrial workers who are so capable of carrying on this work, and I know considerable pressure was brought to bear upon the minister, so that in due course they were able to persuade him that these things could be done. I wish that the minister had, in his report, made reference to the loyalty of the heads of industiy and the great body of workers in industry, because I believe that was due them, as I think the minister will probably agree. The minister rather gave the impression that what has been done was largely as a result of the efforts of his department; but I want to say publicly, knowing something of the situation, that it took some persuasion on the part of heads of industry to make, probably not the minister, but his department realize what could be done in Canada, as shown by what has eventually been done.
Passing on to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald)

and referring briefly to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), I think this house was deeply appreciative of the clear and concise statements given by the ministers of those departments, on whom rests so much responsibility. I do not believe that the country at large or this house were particularly enthusiastic about the explanations given by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) although I pay him this tribute, that he is now, at long last, doing a better job in trying to coordinate the interests of the farming community. I have, however, heard a good deal of critcism of the tactics employed by him in his address. That criticism was made to me both by letter and in person. Then, when we come to the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Crerar)-well, I think the press said enough about that. Those of us who observed the attitude of the minister when he spoke in the house the other day, and compared that with his record, realize that it does not carry much weight with the Canadian people.
This debate awakens strange thoughts in our minds. The security of this country is threatened from both without and within. It is threatened from without by the fiendish activities of the nazis and fascists and by the atrocities that are being perpetrated in the world. I fear it, threatened as it is from within by the practice of political expediency right down to the present moment. No nation can survive when it is attacked from without and from within; no nation, young or old, can survive attacks of those kinds.
I rise in my place in this house for one of several reasons. I read carefully the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon the second reading of this bill. At page 3237 of Hansard for June 10 I find these words:
It is not only the right but it is a duty of hon. members to interpret the view of their constituents, but it is equally a duty in so doing to see that a construction is not placed upon their views which was never and could never have been intended.
That was the first challenge thrown out by the Prime Minister to the members of this house. Then, as reported at page 3235 of Hansard the right hon. gentleman said:
What really is important is that the government's policy should be fully known, presented to parliament, and agreed to by parliament before any action is taken. In this way and in this way only, the people's representatives in parliament can be afforded a full opportunity to discuss the whole subject upon its merits.
The only exception I take to that statement is that here we have a bare bill purporting to give the government an authority which the people of Canada undoubtedly wished the

Mobilization Act-Mr. Lockhart
government to have; yet in the words of the Prime Minister we are told that it may never be necessary to have any form of compulsory service for overseas.
I now pass on to another remark by the Prime Minister, dealing with the plebiscite. These were his words, as reported at page 3231 of Hansard'.
If there be any wisdom in removing false impressions, surely the sooner they are removed the better.
With that I entirely agree, and I say there have been altogether too many false impressions attempted to be put over on the Canadian public.
I now quote briefly from page 3233 of Hansard, where the Prime Minister, after saying that the government had full power to deal with this matter as and when it desired to do so, notwithstanding the provisions of section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act, went on to say:
Why then, it will be asked, does the government come to parliament for powers which it already possesses? The answer to this question is the sense the executive has of its responsibility to parliament.
After this address by the Prime Minister I thought perhaps it would be advisable for me to state what I believe to be the interpretation that was placed upon the plebiscite vote in my constituency, and also to make some brief observations on the general situation that has developed in this House of Commons. As reported at page 3231 of Hansard the Prime Minister stated that it was difficult enough, in some quarters, to have the people sue the wisdom of trusting the government, and he went on to ask, "Why arouse suspicions?" That is what I find in the hearts of a great many of the people. They are suspicious, and I do not believe the debate which has developed here has done much to remove that suspicion.
But let me pass on and state what I believe the people felt was the correct interpretation of the plebiscite vote. They appeared to feel that it was an evasion of responsibility. That statement has been made several times in this house, and I believe that was in the hearts and minds of a good many people. Personally I opposed the taking of the plebiscite. Had the Prime Minister agreed to add the words, "in any theatre of war", as one amendment suggested, the whole situation would have been clarified in the minds of the people. Notwithstanding the fact that the question was vague and uncertain, after it was decided to hold the plebiscite large numbers of my constituents said to me, "What do you propose to do in connection with the vote that is to be taken?"
I must confess, Mr Speaker, and I readily admit, that I was somewhat at a loss to know just what one should do. When I told them that I felt a "yes" vote was absolutely necessary, of course I was immediately asked, "What does a 'yes' vote mean?" Naturally I could not answer that, but I urged my people to do their utmost to get out and vote, and the results were quite obvious in my constituency. The thing I deplored most of all was the loss of a month of valuable time, when Canada's very destiny was hanging in the balance. But then, when I contemplated how that month was being used by members of this house and citizens at large in certain parts of Canada, it dawned upon me that there was the possibility of a "no" vote throughout this country unless the people who would vote "yes" were stirred to get out and cast their ballots as they were expected to do. I say the indifference of the people up to that point was appalling, but it would have been a national tragedy if a decisive "no" vote had been recorded in one part of Canada, while the people in the rest of the country remained indifferent to the whole question.
In any event, the plebiscite was held, and the results have been published. I suppose all hon. members have copies of the Canada Gazette of June 23, which indicates where the "yes" vote was recorded and where the "no" vote was cast. I do not know of anyone on this side of the house who evaded his responsibility. I know that personally I consulted with the other groups represented in my constituency. We held joint meetings, and did our utmost to get the people to vote, notwithstanding the feeling of suspicion and the many criticisms that were voiced against such a vague question. In that plebiscite eight of the nine provinces voted "yes" with a very large majority. I am going to join with the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) by saying that not only in my constituency, but in very many others with which I have been in touch, that was the feeling they had. They were voting on the definite principle of conscription, "yes" or "no", and they expected there would be some definite action in the light of the circumstances developing in this country almost hourly. So I say that the hon. member for Trinity stated quite clearly the condition with

respect not only to his own but to other constituencies. I know of some other constituencies in Canada the representatives of which, if they had the courage of their convictions to tell the story as they know it to be back home, would speak definitely in this debate.

It had to do with letters being received from overseas referring to men with very little training being sent-and they are still being sent to fill the ranks over there. It was only two or three weeks ago I received a letter from a young chap who lives in Windsor, and who is now in England, pointing out that for some reason men were being sent over who had scarcely any training. I would say that this does not represent a healthy state of mind for our men overseas, when the enemy is coming closer and closer to our very shores -in fact, has now reached our coasts.
This all develops into a question of leadership in Canada. I am a comparatively new member in the House of Commons, but I have read a good deal of the past debates. After the Prime Minister made his long speech in moving the second reading of the bill, I spent some time studying the plebiscite of 1917 to which reference has been made by some hon. member's. I shall not do it, because, seriously, I think it is too late. A situation has now been created. It took a number of years to create it, and now it has to be faced as it is. I for one gave warning in this house, and some of my colleagues did the same thing; some of my friends outside this house gave warning that certain causes of discontent and friction should be made to disappear, but nothing was done. I say it is too late now to change the situation, and it must be faced as it is.
I cannot refrain from recounting a conversion which took place between two friends, which may have some bearing on the present case. Two friends met; one said to the other, "Do you think the medicine of Doctor Jones is good?" The other said, "I do not think it is unless you follow the directions very closely." And the first one asked, "What are the directions?" The answer was, "Always keep the bottle tightly corked."
(Translation): Before concluding my remarks on Bill No. 80, I wish to refer to the speech delivered here about two weeks ago by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy). The house undoubtedly listened with sadness, as did all the representatives of the province of Quebec, to the hon. member's inopportune, unjustified and harsh denunciation of the former Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin). Attacking without the slightest provocation, the hon. member for Gaspe worked himself up to a rage where, lacking parliamentary expressions, he resorted to others less dignified. More than once was the Speaker compelled to make him retract his words. Now in critical times such as these, when political partisanship should rightly disappear, at a moment when it is disappearing from the discussion of an essential problem, we can only deplore that the hon. member for Gaspe should have seen fit to depreciate the independence of mind and moral courage shown by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres in quitting his post as Minister of Public Works in the federal cabinet.
The hon. member for Gaspe struck a sour note. He merely succeeded in lowering himself in the esteem of his fellow-citizens of Quebec* both Liberal and Conservative. He has turned himself into the symbol or prototype of that far too numerous class of people who always decry those who meet with success, who cannot suffer one of our men to succeed, and who never miss an opportunity of reviling those who surpass them or of belittling that which God has made great.
These same people, Mr. Speaker, even criticized the sensible, energetic and appropriate speech that the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) recently gave in this house. They criticized that speech of the Minister of Justice in which he was noble and impartial enough to advise his followers, his colleagues and his friends in the house to vote according to the dictates of their conscience instead of urging them to follow his lead, an advice he might very well have given them. I wish to protest against these malevolent and unbecoming criticisms which can serve no useful purpose.
Mr. Speaker, there is no need of speaking at length to explain our stand on the amendment to the Mobilization Act. Indeed were the length of the speeches measured by that of the amendment, it soon would be disposed of; in fact, one short sentence is the object of this debate, to wit: section 3 of this act is repealed. Our participation in the war in 1939 and the Mobilization Act in 1940 were willingly accepted by all of us following official representations and statements by our ministers, which I shall not quote, precisely because of section 3 of the Mobilization Act which reads as follows:
The powers conferred by the next preceding section may not be exercised for the purpose of requiring persons to serve in the military, naval or air forces outside of Canada and the territorial waters thereof.
That clause shut the door on conscription for overseas service. We were satisfied and quite prepared to continue making sacrifices. I see a grave danger in the disappearance of that clause notwithstanding what the government give us to understand. I may as well say, Mr. Speaker, that the Quebec people, if I am to judge by the feeling in my constituency, under no consideration will accept compulsion for service overseas; I repeat under no consideration. Being anxious to

Mobilization Act-Mr. Brunette
state the views of my electors and quite unwilling to deceive those who have been conscripted solely for home defence, mindful also of the pledges I gave my electors, I cannot agree to the repeal of clause 3, our sole guarantee against overseas service.
I supported the holding a plebiscite because it was a means of sampling the opinion of the people, a substantially democratic measure allowing the people to express their will freely. I can now say that at least 95 per cent of my constituents decided not to release the government from its pledge nor to free me from my own commitments. Had they done so, I would nonetheless vote against conscription, for I believe in persuasion and not in compulsion.
I am not ashamed of my own or my electors' stand on this issue, neither am I afraid of voicing my opinion because I feel that we are not alone in that position. It has been pointed out repeatedly, and I wish to recall it once again, that Australia, Northern Ireland, South Africa and India do not have conscription for service outside their borders. When embittered, fanatical and evil Canadian citizens, of the same ilk as Dr. Shields, of Toronto, who does not hesitate to use his church pulpit for the purpose of raising the year round, on fifty-two consecutive Sundays, the race cry in this country, when Canadian citizens preach hatred, discord and intolerance instead of charity and harmony, such people should ask themselves, before blaming the Prime Minister for not enforcing conscription in Quebec, if the province of Quebec does anything to prevent them from adopting conscription for themselves.
Mr. Speaker, I find it quite strange that a congregation of serious and intelligent people should let their pastor use his church pulpit every Sunday of the year for the purpose of raising the race cry, of delivering political speeches and slavering over a quarter of our population at a time when unity is so necessary in this dominion. Mr. Speaker, there are many kinds of fifth columnists. Racial conditions being what they are in this country, the actions of Dr. Shields, of Toronto, are those of a fifth columnist. I know it is not advisable as a rule to publicize the doings of miscreants, but I believe it is high time that this notorious pastor were denounced because our silence might be misconstrued as an admission of the truth of his statements.
If conscription does not follow the passing of this amendment, so much the better, and I pray God that the Prime Minister may hold his ground and succeed in silencing the advocates of conscription in this country. I do not hesitate to say that I shall always trust the 
Prime Minister but unfortunately he is not the only member of his cabinet and he will not live forever. For those reasons I am quite dubious about this amendment.
I notice with much regret, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative and conscriptionist opposition, so talkative and politically-minded, is winning another hand in the conscription game. Though that opposition is not powerful, it has but a handful of members, it proves once again that the least useful wheel is the most creaky. I am prepared to admit that some of them are sincere but I believe that most are prompted by other motives and that political sonsiderations have much to do with, if they not wholly explain their attitude. Since 1939 they have been complaining about everything and everybody and they always fall back on conscription with the sole object of embarrassing the Prime Minister whose views in the matter they know, and of dividing the Liberal party in the province of Quebec. Their efforts are well known.
I would even state that in the province of Quebec there are rabid politicians who, while they fear conscription like -the very devil, would be satisfied to see the government enforce it so that they might derive some political advantage therefrom. What a shame to deal so lightly with such a grave question! But our Conservative friends in Quebec have once more chosen the wrong path, for the Liberal members from the province of Quebec, almost to a man, wishing to honour their promises, will keep the pledges given to their constituents, will oppose this conscription measure to the bitter end by voting first of all against the amendment to the mobilization act. Sincere opinions deserve to be respected as does a firm attitude consistently held. For perseverance and tenacity are often a proof of sincerity. But what spectacle are the Conservatives giving us? Their only evident consistency since 1939 has been a ceaseless attempt to destroy the Prime Minister and to belittle Canada's vast and admirable war effort.
A wise man makes no statement without substantiating it. I intend quoting evidence gathered at random in the several sessions held since the outbreak of hostilities, to show that while regularly urging the adoption of conscription, the Conservatives mainly attempted to play politics and to have the Canadian people lose confidence in the present government. You shall see, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservatives are opportunists and seek only political advantage.
During one of these sessions, while offering us a side-dish of conscription, they launched their main attack or offensive to form a national government. And we saw the Con-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Farquhar
servatives, who could not reach power the normal way, endeavour to get there through charity's door. They clamored that the best men should be placed at the helm, in order that they might obtain at least a part of the spoils of war they had found so fruitful in 1914 and 1918. But they were on the wrong track and got nowhere.
At another session, they criticized the government because it did not send a sufficient number of men overseas and because our war munitions output was not high enough. After the matter had been debated for at least a week, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) made his statement and I can still hear the opposition leader (Mr. Hanson) confessing that he had spoken rashly and that Canada's war effort was, after all, an admirable one.
Later on the conscription issue was raised again. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, those bitter denunciations of the Prime Minister. How comical they all appeared, rising one after the other to say that the Prime Minister was a great man, an honest man and an able administrator to boot, but adding that he was not one to wage war, not a wartime Prime Minister; he lacked the necessary qualities of leadership.
However, the Prime Minister has succeeded in being elected three times to his present high post and the third time he commanded the greatest majority obtained since confederation.
At another session, the interim leader of the opposition, sickened by his failure and aware, after a tour of the country, that the Canadian people opposed conscription for overseas service, tendered his resignation which was immediately if not blithely accepted by his colleagues. The Hon. Arthur Meighen, branded as a thoroughbred conscriptionist, left the Senate well determined to come to this House so as to set things in order and hasten the passing of conscription for overseas service. This was a cause of great rejoicing for the loyalists and the opposition. The campaign in York South was memorable. There were severe accusations against the government for their sluggishness, and against the Prime Minister because he had not assumed the portfolio of war; this was followed by a thorough defeat and the complete crushing of the hopes of the Hon. Arthur Meighen.
At another session, the debate was on selective service. No more was said about conscription for the word had become a bogey. Mr. Speaker, I shall give you my candid opinion on this matter. I feel that selective service, might be a very good system, in a country as populous as the United States, but
that, in a country like Canada, whose population is limited, no legislation is necessary to effect a well-balanced distribution of the man-power between army, navy, air force, agriculture and industry.
At still another session, the opposition complained that the Department of National Defence was not putting the Canadian army to work. They claimed that our army was shamefully idle, that our men did not compare with the Australian soldiers; then, England invited the Department of National Defence to send a contingent to Hong Kong. We all know what happened then. Some of our men have died, some have been taken prisoners, all have endured severe hardships. At the next session, the opposition blamed us for having sent troops to Hong Kong.
Mr. Speaker, whatever the calibre of the opposition, they have made considerable progress and I must admit that the idea of conscription has had some success. They keep repeating that our fighting troops overseas are not numerous enough and in the same breath, they complain of the lack of men on the farms and on the industrial front.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill No. 80 to repeal section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act has, in my opinion, taken up altogether too much time. I intend to touch briefly on only two or three points.
Speaking in the house on the plebiscite bill on March 12, I said that I was not opposed to conscription, if and when conscription became necessary. I stated further that I did not think conscription was necessary at that time. I know of no reason why I should change my mind now.
I have listened carefully to the address of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and those of many other hon. members, and I find no suggestion that the voluntary enlistment system has failed in xny way. Nor have they given any reason to show that conscription is necessary at the present time. I wish every person in Canada would read the address delivered by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) on Tuesday of last week. If his observations were read by all our people, I believe they would be convinced that what we need and what we have is a well-balanced war effort. The minister pointed out that conscription was not the all-

Mobilization Act-Mr. Farquhar
important factor. He showed clearly that one of the great problems was the manufacturing of war munitions, and the building of ships to transport those munitions to our allies who are in such great need of them.
All hon. members know that Russia has far more trained men in reserve than Germany has. If Russia to-day could get enough heavy equipment such as tanks, heavy guns and aeroplanes, she could drive every German out of her country, and defeat Germany on her own soil. I read a report recently which stated that China has five million men at the battle front, and that she has ten million trained men in reserve. But these men cannot get the arms with which to fight. Just think of it! Ten million men, equal in number almost to the population of Canada; all these men, but unarmed 1 They are crying for arms, but cannot get them.
The same is true of Libya. If our armies in Libya to-day could have had all the heavy equipment and tanks and guns and aeroplanes they required they would not have been driven back, sixty miles into Egypt, as is reported in to-day's press. India is in the same position. She has unlimited numbers of men, but cannot get the equipment. The United States is raising an army of ten million men. That country is shipping all possible war materials out of the country, and sending them to India, China, Libya-almost every country in the world. If Great Britain could obtain the heavy equipment, tanks, heavy guns and all other necessary war equipment, we would have a second front to-day, and would be closing in on the Germans from the west.
In these times the all-important task in Canada is not the conscription of men for overseas service. There is something to be proud of in the fact that over half a million men have volunteered for service anywhere in the world. Two days ago the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) had this to say:
I always prefer to see our Canadian army overseas a purely volunteer army.
Would not anyone be proud to say that our army overseas was entirely and purely a volunteer army? I trust that when this war is ended Canada will be able to say with pride that not one man had to be forced into service; that every man overseas was a volunteer.
It has been said in this house that there are two extreme views on this question of conscription. To my mind both are wrong. As has been pointed out, the one extreme view is that there should be conscription at any cost, regardless of what effect it may have upon our unity or war effort. The other 
extreme view is that we should not have conscription under any circumstances. There are many who are opposed to this system of conscription. Sir Wilfrid Laurier held that view; the late Ernest Lapointe held that view; the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) holds that view, and many other outstanding leaders in the province of Quebec are of the same mind. Will anyone doubt the sincerity or the loyalty of these men? Can it be expected that men of French origin will have the same feeling toward Great Britain as Canadians of British stock have? I often feel that people in other provinces are most unfair in their judgment of the people of Quebec.
It is difficult to understand the attitude of the opposition group on this question of conscription. When the plebiscite vote was taken Liberals, Conservatives, the members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation-I am not so sure of the Social Credit group-all united in an effort to convince the people of Canada that they were not voting on the question of conscription. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Hanson), and the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group (Mr. Coldwell) said so. We said so in our broadcasts; we said so in our letters to the press, and we said so from the public platform. We did everything we possibly could to convince the people of Canada that they were not voting on conscription.
Having some confidence in us, the people of Canada came out and voted "yes" in large numbers. It is true that those who were voting for conscription voted "yes", but it is also true that thousands and thousands of people voted in the belief that we were sincere. Many, if not all of the members of the opposition, and the odd Liberal member interpreted that vote as a vote for conscription. What changed their minds over night?
I do not know, but I do know that they must admit one of two things. They must admit that they were sincere but that their people had no confidence in them, or they must admit that they were not sincere and tried deliberately to mislead the people of Canada.
That is one reason why the Conservative party is in the position in which it finds itself to-day. Can any party expect to have the confidence of the people of Canada when their word does not mean anything? Speaking in this debate, the leader of the opposition brought up once again the question of a national government, and he is reported on page 3249 of Hansard as follows:
I believe now, as I have believed from the outset, that the highest efficiency in carrying

Mobilization Act-Mr. McDonald
out such a programme can be guaranteed only by the establishment of a truly national government, a government composed of the best men in Canada, representative of all shades of opinion, but united by a common and single purpose-the waging of total war by total effort.
I have urged this view many times in this house.
I emphatically reiterate it to-day. More than ever am I convinced that unity of purpose and action will be achieved only under such a policy and position.
I have no doubt that there are capable men in the Conservative ranks who would be qualified to fill the positions they might be called upon to fill in a national government, but in discussing this question of a national government there is one thing that the leader of the opposition and his followers overlook. In order to form a national government it would be necessary to elect the members. If the leader of the opposition is honest-and 1 believe he is-he will agree with me when I say that it is very hard to elect a Conservative anywhere in Canada to-day. Surely the leader of the opposition and his followers have not forgotten how the people of Canada refused to accept national government at the last election. Surely they have not forgotten how the people in one of thte strongest Conservative ridings in Ontario said of one of the strongest and ablest men in the party, "We do not want him at any price." In the face of these facts, I suggest to the leader of the opposition and his followers that they forget forever the question of national government. The Conservative party can never expect to regain the confidence of the people of Canada so long as they use the tactics they are using at present in connection with this question of conscription.
I said that I was going to be very brief, and I shall close with these words: Any member of this house, I care not to what party he belongs, who now interprets the affirmative vote on the plebiscite as a vote for conscription-after he and his party definitely said that it was not-and advocates conscription on the strength of that vote, has broken faith with the people of Canada and is ho longer worthy of the confidence that his electors placed in him.
