speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like all the other bon. members who have spoken, I consider it is clearly my duty on this occasion to present my views on this important issue and to state what will be my attitude toward the amendment at present before the house.
As you know, I am one of the members from the province of Quebec. I am not a French-Canadian member. There is not a drop of French-Canadian blood in my veins. But I do know something of Quebec and of
the French Canadians whom I have had the privilege to represent in the legislature of my native province as well as in this house.
On the plebiscite issue I did my utmost in my humble way to obtain, if possible, a "yes" vote, with a pretty good idea beforehand what my efforts would mean. The result was that there was a large "no" vote in my constituency. I was not disappointed. During the Easter recess I made several speeches over the radio in connection with the plebiscite vote, and I took occasion to tell the people of my riding that a "yes" vote on the plebiscite did not necessarily mean a vote for conscription. I went further; I told them distinctly, for reasons which I shall explain later in my speech, that I had been opposed to conscription in the past, was opposed to conscription at that particular time, and would continue to be opposed to it. So you can conclude, sir, from these remarks that, since the amendment contained in the bill before us to-day involves the principle of conscription, I cannot in conscience vote for that amendment; and when I say that, I do it with the utmost regret, because for the first time in my public life of-now-twenty-three years, I shall have to cast a vote of want of confidence against my party and against the leader in whom, apart from this particular issue, I have confidence.
I have said that I am a member from the province of Quebec, and I have sat and listened to derogatory remarks made by members of the opposition-I am sorry that more of them are not in their seats at the present time, because I have something to say to them-about Quebec and the attitude of its members and its people with regard to the war and to conscription.
The hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) yesterday afternoon said, among other things:
. . . the view of national unity held by hon. members from Quebec is that the other eight provinces must bow to their will.
Evidently we members from the province of Quebec are supermen and are quite capable of exercising our will and superiority over the great majority of the members of this house. I appreciate the compliment, coming from the hon. member. He also made some other allusions to the province of Quebec, and I shall answer them as I go along in my speech.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce), in his usual ingratiating manner, referred this afternoon to Quebec's perverse education at the hands of politicians. I am quite willing

Mobilization Act-Mr. McDonald
to admit, sir, that Quebec has received perverse education at the hands of certain politicians, not, however, members of the Liberal party, and I intend to prove that from certain historical papers which I have before me.
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) said to-night that the leadership of the province of Quebec is such that the people of Quebec are to-day paying the price for it.
Let us see something of the so-called leadership on this particular issue that the people of Quebec have been receiving, these hon. members say, for the last twenty-five years. I hold in my hand excerpts of articles taken from Le Devoir under date of May 29, 1913, signed by Henri Bourassa, who at that time was the owner and editor of this newspaper. Mr. Bourassa was at that time also the leader of the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec. He had broken away from Sir Wilfrid Laurier over the South African war and formed a party of Nationalists in our province. In 1910 a by-election was held in the constituency of Drummond-Arthabaska, in the province of Quebec, in which by-election the Nationalist party for the first time presented a candidate. The doctrine that they preached to the people of that constituency in the by-election was not one of participation in the wars of the British empire or in wars outside Canada; quite the contrary. They said, "If you return Laurier and Laurier's candidate to power, you encourage him to car-y on his naval bill", which at that time he had before parliament; "he will conscript your sons, place them on these vessels which he is going to build, and send them over all the seas of the world to fight in England's wars, and they will be engaged in every war in which the empire takes part." The appeal went home. While the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier at that time was very strong, particularly in the province of Quebec, Mr. Bourassa's candidate was elected by a majority of something over 200 votes. That was the first test of the Nationalist party in the province of Quebec.
Then came the general election of 1911. It was supposed to be fought out on the reciprocity issue, but the issue in the province of Quebec was not reciprocity; it was Laurier's naval bill, and Mr. Bourassa and his candidates of the Nationalist party took part in that election. Now we get the story, as printed in this newspaper Le Devoir, of what occurred. Probably it would have never come to light had it not been for the fact that, when these gentlemen eventually were elected and attained power, they forgot the promises they 
made to Mr. Bourassa and, in order to retain office, remained within the ranks of the Conservative party.
Then the plot was exposed. That is the reason why for some time we have been able to know what took place. We know now about the loyalty of the Conservative party; we know what party flag-wavers they are, and we know that in the election of 1911 their candidates were strutting up and down Ontario, with a flag wrapped round them, saying to the people of that province, "No truck or trade with the Yankees; President Taft says that if this treaty passes, Canada will become a political adjunct of the United States." But, Mr. Speaker, that was not what was taking place in the province of Quebec; it was something entirely different. Here is part of the story. The first article is on May 29, 1913:
The Conservatives solicit the help of the Nationalists.
Mr. Bourassa is writing:
Not being a party, we will not have a candidate in the ranks; but we will support any candidate, Liberal or Conservative, for or against reciprocity, who will at first hand promise to fight any policy of participation, direct or indirect, in the wars of the empire outside of Canada, or at least who will promise to repulse any measure of this kind before the people have been consulted by means of a plebiscite; and in such a case we will consult neither the wishes nor the interests of one or the other party. We wish-and this is no secret-to obtain the election of enough independent members to overthrow the navy bill and all other means of contributing to imperial armaments just as long as the people have not stated their will in the matter.
There was the first step towards the agreement with our friends the Conservatives. He goes on:
It is up to Mr. Borden and his lieutenants to decide whether they will allow the election of the candidates we support or begin a tripartite fight which will assure the election of the ministerial candidates. In those electoral districts where the fight will take place between orthodox Liberals and Conservatives we will let them fight amongst themselves.
They were not interested in that. They arranged that no candidates should be placed in the field under the name of Conservatives or anything else, except these Nationalists,
, and he goes on to state that one good Conservative had to make room for a Nationalist candidate because the organizer of the Nationalist party arranged for his withdrawal. You know the old saying, Mr. Speaker, that elections are not won by prayers, and the Nationalist candidates were quite able men on the platform, but they were not gifted overmuch with this world's goods. Hence, finances were somewhat of a necessity. Mr. Bourassa says:

Mobilization Act-Mr. McDonald
Besides the protestations of faith, the speeches and courtesies of the candidates, there remained the very important question of electoral funds, that festering sore of politics. In this regard the Nationalists were of no help. They furnished the ideas, the enthusiasm and the popularity, hut that was all they could give. The organizers of the autonomous party

That is the Nationalist party.
-had offered their moneys, those willing and able to subscribe to the opposition's election funds. There were a certain number who shared Mr. Monk's opinions on the naval question; others thought only of reciprocity; the shade of the candidates they helped was a matter of indifference to them provided they were opposed to the customs convention; others only wished the overthrow of the government, no matter what the ideas or principles of the opposition, whether with regard to the navy or reciprocity.
So they contributed their funds to help the Nationalist party to be elected; and when the regular funds were exhausted another gentleman who had a long purse, a man prominent in the' Conservative party in Quebec, appeared upon the scene with some additional funds. He wanted to take notes payable from candidates and they refused to deal with him; consequently he had to accede to the wishes of the candidates and supply the money without receiving the notes. Mr. Bourassa goes on to say:
The fact remains that the Conservative party funds and the imperial treasury helped to defray the election dues of from thirty to forty candidates for or against reciprocity, who denounced the navy bill, and the "no less nefarious" policy of Mr. Borden, and who solemnly pledged themselves to vote against any government that refused to allow a plebiscite on this question.
The Tories at that time went about their work very thoroughly. They had contributed directly to the funds, but they saw another opportunity. Mr. Bourassa, as I have stated, was also proprietor and editor of a newspaper, Le Devoir which is still in existence, but which at that time had not anything like the circulation which it has to-day; nor had it the weight or the importance which attaches to it at the present time. So they conceived the idea that it would be good 'business to get a more extensive circulation of the newspaper in the province of Quebec in order to extend the propaganda through the paper, in addition to the speeches on the platform, and Mr. Bourassa relates how this was brought about. In an article dated Tuesday, June 3, 1913, he says;
Some days afterwards one of the most important heads of the Conservative committee, armed with electoral lists of all the eastern counties, obtained subscriptions to Le Devoir for the duration of the campaign from a few thousand of these brave electors. At any rate, we were princely. Par from taking advantage 44561-235
of the situation and holding up these gentlemen, the paper gave them generous terms; we only asked for the price of the regular subscription-
They did not charge them anything extra, just the regular subscription.
-minus the commission usually paid to regular solicitors.
They were generous.
We thus remained free from anything that looked like political subscription and we had the paramount satisfaction-
This is rich.
-of having the mammon of Tory imperialistic iniquity served to spread the good Nationalist doctrine in full columns.
Mr. Bourassa was making such good progress in the province of Quebec that his fame had spread even to the loyal province of Ontario. I am surprised to read-but of course I knew of it at the time, because I was taking part in that campaign-that he had received an invitation to visit the good loyal province of Ontario and propagate there his good loyal doctrine of nationalism that he was preaching in the province of Quebec. He had a visit from certain gentlemen of Ontario while he was attending a meeting at St. Hyacinthe. His answer was not quite satisfactory to the delegation that waited upon him, so one day he was shown a telegram which was addressed to Mr. McCrea. Mr. McCrea had been told that Mr. Bourassa would not go to Ontario unless certain explicit promises were made by the candidates, so Mr. McCrea evidently wired the candidates and received replies reading as follows:
Mattawa, Ontario,
September 8, 1911.
I certainly am opposed to the reciprocity pact and the navy policy of the government and will support a request for repeal of naval policy and a referendum to the people no matter who is premier.
That was signed by George Gordon, the senator who died recently, who was then a candidate for Nipissing. A similar telegram was also sent by a Mr. Smith.
Being assured by these gentlemen that they would carry out their obligation, Mr. Bourassa consented to visit Ontario and propagate his good, loyal doctrine in that good, loyal province. Here is his reference to the effect of his visit there:
I spoke in Sudbury on September 18. This was the most clearly nationalistic, the most flatly anti-imperialistic speech of all those I delivered during the campaign. Since that time the Hon. Mr. Cochrane, known to be sparing of words and praises, honoured me by saying that my arguments made an even more marked impression on English-speaking electors than on French Canadians.



Mobilization Act-Mr. McDonald
He made more converts in Ontario than in Quebec.

speechtext:
The result of the elections in Quebec was as follows. On the dissolution of the house the Liberal party had fifty seats; all other groups had fifteen. After the election the Liberals had thirty-seven seats; the Nationalists had twenty-seven, and there was one Independent, making a total of sixty-five. So that victory in Quebec brought about the balance of power which overthrew the Laurier administration and elected Mr. Borden.
More striking than that are the figures of the popular vote. The Liberal party in that election obtained 164,281 votes. The opposition, the Nationalists, had 159,299. The popular vote in the province of Quebec was split practically fifty-fifty between the Nationalists and the Liberals.
That is what we have had to contend with in the province of Quebec from 1911 down to the present time. That is the element we have to fight, and that is the element .which is responsible for what the opposition accuse us of, the wrong leadership in the province of Quebec. My charge is that in 1911 they betrayed every principle of decency; they sold out their party in order to gain a cheap victory, and to-day they are trying to cast that onus and aspersion on the Liberals because, they say, Quebec does not measure up to their expectations.
In a moment I am going to refer to some of the things that were said by one of those men who was afterwards taken into the cabinet. These men who preached doctrines in the province of Quebec which were practically seditious, financed by Conservative money, were taken into the cabinet of Sir Robert Borden in 1911: L. P. Pelletier, Postmaster General; T. D. Monk, Public Works; Bruno Nantel, Minister of National Revenue; and P. E. Blondin, Deputy Speaker, who had a particular flair for shooting holes in the British flag.
Before- the term of that parliament had expired, war had broken out. But before that time, Mr. Borden introduced his naval bill for a contribution of $35,000,000 to the British navy. In view of the speeches that these men and other supporters of the Borden administration in the province of Quebec had made, they should have resigned their seats, unless they had a plebiscite of the people. But they hung on to office; office was sweet; they stayed until the expiration of parliament in 1917. There were

changes in the administration during that time. Mr. Nantel, who had been Minister of Inland Revenue, had been named a judge; he was replaced by Mr. Blondin, who became Minister of Inland Revenue in 1914. He was introduced into this house in 1915 by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, a great imperialist, Sir George Foster. I am going to leave it to Sir Wilfrid Laurier to say how he, Mr. Blondin, was introduced. Sir Wilfrid said, in a manner that only Laurier possessed, as reported at page 209 of Hansard of 1915:
Mr. Nantel also has been called away from the floor of parliament and removed to another sphere. It is not my intention to say anything of the removal of Mr. Nantel from office, but I may have something to say as to the choice of his successor, the present incumbent of the office, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Blondin). It seemed an evidence of the irony of fate that the hon. member for Champlain, the arch-Nationalist, should have been introduced to the house by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), the arch-imperialist. When on the opening of the session, I saw the new minister walking into this house leaning upon the arm of my hon friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I thought the Minister of Trade and Commerce showed by the way he seemed to be limping that he had a heavy load to carry. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has always been an insistent advocate of imperialism. I cannot say as much of his new colleague; but perhaps, after all, there may be within the ranks of the Conservative party, as there is somewhere else, some joy over the conversion of one sinner. The Minister of Inland Revenue was introduced by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce. When he told you, sir, that the hon. gentleman had taken the oath and had signed the roll, I thought he would add that the hon. gentleman had filled up the holes in the flag and that he would now breath the atmosphere of liberty. But he did not, and really there was no necessity for his doing so. The hon. member for Champlain is now breathing the atmosphere of office; he has found an atmosphere which is suitable to him, and he can breathe freely, whether there are holes in the flag or not. I have only this to observe: when my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue, then the hon. member for Champlain, was making the speeches which he did make in the province of Quebec; when he was threatening to destroy the Canadian navy when he had an opportunity of doing so, I never believed that he meant one-half of what he said. I always supposed, and rightly supposed, that what he was after was to create advantage for himself and for his party. He has succeeded. He is now in office, but to attain office he has travelled a very dangerous road. He has sown the seed of discord-and these appeals to passion are always sure to bring forth a crop of prejudices. My hon. friend, the Minister of Inland Revenue, is a young member of this house; perhans he will permit me to say, since now he has the responsibility of office, that he had better always stand by true principle.

Mobilization Act-Mr. McDonald
May I direct those words to the Conservative party. It might be better for them to stand by true principle, and lay the responsibility for wrong leadership in the province of Quebec where it properly belongs, instead of attempting to lay it upon the ministers and humble members of the Liberal party who come from that province. Personally I have been fighting the battles of the Liberal party in Quebec for forty years, and I have no apology to make to anyone for the sort of fight I have put up there. I have used conscription as an argument because conscription was imposed upon the people of Canada, and especially upon us in the province of Quebec, in 1917 for no other purpose than to win an election for a government that had lost every vestige of the confidence of the people of Canada. The shameful arguments that were used in the other provinces against us; the shameful announcements which were made,, some of which I quoted during my speech here in February, as I said on that occasion and repeat to-ndght were seared' into my memory. I have had no apology to offer, nor have I to-night, for any statement I have made in the past or for any statements I may make in the future in carrying on that campaign in the province of Quebec as long as there is a Tory who shows his face in that province. Little did they dream in 1911, when they were carrying on this campaign to split our people in two on this question of the naval bill and the contribution to imperial wars, that in 1914 war would break out and that between 1914 and 1917 they would be asking the people of Quebec to support the war effort and enlist as those in the other provinces were doing. To-day they are reaping the results of their actions, and theirs is the responsibility.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I come to the present war. In my speech in February I stated that since the declaration of war Quebec has done its share in comparison with the other provinces. I am just as firmly convinced of that to-night, and as a member from Quebec I have no apologies to offer, nor am I blushing over the part my province has taken. I have before me the speech of the late lamented Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe, delivered in this house on September 9, 1939, in which he outlined the programme, the sentiment and the feelings of the people of Quebec; not with the idea, as the hon. member for Hastings-Peter-borough suggested yesterday, of imposing the will of the people of Quebec upon the other provinces, but as the feelings of a sister province, willing to take her share of responsibility along with the other provinces of this dominion. As reported at page 68 of Hansard for 44561-2351
September 9, 1939, Mr. Lapointe used these words:
The whole province of Quebec-and I speak with all the responsibility and all the solemnity I can give to my words-will never agree to accept compulsory service or conscription outside Canada. I will go farther than that: When I say the whole province of Quebec I mean that I personally agree with them.
Then he went on:
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is it not worth while to the Canadian nation, when the nation is at war, to preserve unity on the side on which Canada will be-this unity which is represented by the province of Quebec in the government- behind the measures being taken to help our mother country and France? . . .
Provided these points are understood, we are willing to offer our services without limitation and to devote our best efforts for the success of the cause we all have at heart. And those in Quebec who say that we will have conscription, in spite of what some of us are saying, are doing the work of disunity, the work of the foe, the work of the enemy.
Again that same fall of 1939 when the then Premier of Quebec dissolved the legislature and attempted to obtain a new mandate from the people by asking them not to take part in the war our ministers from that province, including Mr. Lapointe, the ex-Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), and the present Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) took part in the campaign. I have before me a newspaper report of a speech delivered by Mr. Lapointe on October 10, 1939, in which he is quoted as having said:
But I have faith in my province. I am confident that it will not render a verdict that will be acclaimed in Berlin and Moscow on election night. Nazi and communist agents have stirred up dissension in all the countries of America. Quebec will not allow itself to be influenced by such propaganda.
And further on he said:
Canada must remain united. Any attempt at breaking that unity is fratricidal and criminal. We must have tolerance and mutual respect.
And again:
I have succeeded in healing many wounds. I have steadfastly held up Canada's banner, convinced as I was that the sacred interests of my province were linked with the preservation of Canadian ideals.
Those were the sentiments of the late Minister of Justice; those were the sentiments of every true Liberal and every Canadian citizen of the province of Quebec at that time; and, Mr. Speaker, those are the sentiments of the true Canadians of Quebec to-day. We do not want or need conscription in the province of Quebec. Quebec is doing its share in this war.
Let me quote an extract from an address given by the Hon. J. Arthur Mathewson, the provincial treasurer of Quebec. It will be

Mobilization Act-Mr. McDonald
noted that he is not a French Canadian. This address was delivered in Montreal on November 25, 1941, and was in part as follows:
So much for what we are doing in a material way. Now what about man-power? Quebec can justly boast that it provided the first full regiment of infantry in all Canada. It was a Freneh-Canadian regiment. It was recruited to full strength under its gallant leader, Colonel Robert Bourassa, himself a veteran of the last war, and who unfortunately, after proceeding to England with his unit, has now been invalided back and lies here paralyzed. He led the van of Canada in recruiting and the sympathy of all Canadians must go out to him now, to console him in his suffering.
His was the first regiment. The two regiments which followed in recruiting to full strength were one from Ontario and the other one again from the province of Quebec. Several other regiments, both English-Canadian and French Canadian, have gone from this province.
When the recruiting drive was launched last spring, an objective -was set for the province of Quebec. The province met its requirements. The city of Quebec surpassed its quota and achieved 122 per cent.
It would be interesting to the enemy to know exactly how many troops have gone from Quebec. They will not be told. On the other hand Quebec cannot be accused of complacency. We are not complacent.
He concludes with these words:
The French Canadian loves Canada through the province of Quebec, just as a Scotchman loves Britain through his affection for his own native hills. The Grampians and Loch Lomond are to the Scotchman what the Laurentians and the spruce-clad banks of the St. Lawrence are to the French Canadian. That affection for his native - heath is not a detriment-it is a source of vital strength.
Quebec will not fail. Depend upon us and we will not let you down. Know above all that here in Quebec are three million Christian consciences, each one a bastion, a fortress, that Hitler's hordes and their supreme commander, who is Satan, will never conquer.
My time has almost expired, and I should like to conclude with two quotations from a book written, by Pierre Georges Roy and entitled "Les Petites Choses de Notre Histoire." Two articles struck me forcibly while reading them. The first is headed "Nos coeurs a la France; nos bras a l'Angleterre"-"Our hearts belong to France, but our arms belong to England," and is as follows:
What is the origin of these words which express so admirably the feeling of the great majority of French Canadians since the day when providence broke the bond which united Canada to France?
On July 13, 1885, for the first time since 1760, a French corvette La Capricieuse entered the port of Quebec. The older people, greatly moved, said that their people had come back and the French officers were welcomed as heroes and applauded wherever they went.
The captain, monsieur de Belveze, visited mademoiselle de Lanaudiere, the daughter of one of the leaders in the battle of the Plains of Abraham-an old lady of eighty-five, with a

very good memory and a wit as sparkling as in the days of her youth. They spoke mostly of France, non' allied by treaty with England, in what has been known during recent years as an "entente cordiale". But like most French naval officers, the captain did not like England, and could not understand the faithful allegiance of the Canadians to England while they professed such a deep love for France. Finally, unable to find a more convincing argument, mademoiselle de Lanaudiere said these words which have become historic: "Our hearts belong to France, but our arms belong to England."
One further quotation from the same source, and I shall have finished. This is headed "Le Dernier Coup de Canon," and is as follows:
During the second session of the second union parliament which was opened on March 29, 1846, by Lord Cathcart, both sides of the house unanimously passed a law to establish the army on a working basis.
Sir Etienne-Paschal Tache, who had fought in 1812, made a patriotic speech in which he assured the house that if the occasion arose, the French Canadians would conduct themselves again in a manner as heroic.
"What our fathers and we ourselves have done to defend the colony," he said, "our children will be found ready to do, if they are considered in a just light. Our loyalty is not one of speculation, of pounds and shillings, and pence. It is not constantly on our lips. We do not make a business of it. Our habits, our laws, our religion, have made us monarchists and conservatives. We only ask to be treated with justice, and if the enemy comes, you will see our battalions, light-hearted and brave, go forth to fight the foe. 'But', our detractors say, 'you are malcontents, it is impossible to reason with you.' "Tou are rebels,' say the ultras, 'we alone possess loyalty to the highest degree.' A thousand pardons, gentlemen, treat us as children of the same mother and not as illegitmate, treat us with more justice in your deeds as well as in your words, and I give you my word that if ever this country ceases to be British, the last cannon shot to maintain British power on American soil will have been fired by a French Canadian."
I commend these quotations to the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO REPEAL SECTION 3 PROVIDING LIMITATION IN RESPECT OF SERVICE OVERSEAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the few moments I have left before eleven o'clock I shall endeavour to make my position clear with respect to the bill now under discussion. I have always been opposed to conscription. On each and every occasion in the past twenty-five or thirty years I have taken the stand I am taking to-night. At every opportunity I have spoken against imposing conscription for service overseas. I have felt this way because I am convinced that the most satisfactory method of recruiting men is under the voluntary system, and I believe that experience gained under the mobilization act has proved I am right.
In Canada the province of Quebec, my native province, and one of which I have a right to be proud, has been accused of not

Mobilization Act

Mr. Mullins
doing its duty. It is clear, however, from figures tabled in the house one day this week that the numbers of French Canadians who have enlisted voluntarily have been very satisfactory indeed. It must not be forgotten that for a country of only between 11,000,000 and 12,000,000 people we have had wonderful success in accomplishing great things in connection with our war endeavour. Other countries have complimented Canada upon the fact that for her size and population she has done more in the way of her war effort than any other country.
It has been said from the opposite side of the house, as well as by other people opposed to this government in politics, that the French Canadians are not doing their share in this war. Such remarks are most unpleasant to the ears of a man who has lived in Quebec all his life and who hopes to pass the rest of his days in that province. I have lived among French-Canadian people, and I do not intend to change my place of abode. They are the finest people in the world. Because of political, and perhaps financial reasons, there are a few in the house and, outside the house, a few in the other provinces who spend their time in knocking Quebec. Why do they seek to divide the country? Is it t<|>
try to ruin the party in power for their own political future?
According to the figures in Hansard, the total enlistments in the three armed forces from Quebec up to the present month were 74,053, of whom 36,140 were French-speaking and 37,913 were English-speaking and all other origins. The total enlistments in the army to serve anywhere from the beginning of the war up to the present month were 29,651 French-speaking and 27,071 Englishspeaking and all other origins. Therefore it would appear that the remarks of these gentlemen are absolutely unfounded and unfair. I repeat that there is only one reason for such arguments, to advance their own political and personal positions, and perhaps in the case of some of them, to ensure their political future.
During the plebiscite campaign I did not try to influence my people. I made no public speeches; I left them free, and they voted 75 per cent "no". I hope that my electors will understand, when I vote against this bill, that I do not do so because of any lack of confidence in my government, but I am confident that the present government will never impose conscription. After section 3 of the National Resources Mobilization Act has been deleted, there will be no opportunity of discussing this matter before conscription is
put into force. I repeat that it is not lack of confidence in my government or my chief that causes me to vote against the government on this measure.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words in French, the native tongue of the majority of my constituents.
(Translation) I have always been opposed to conscription. For the last twenty-five years, on every occasion that offered, I have spoken, in public as in private, against conscription for overseas service. It was not that I was averse to defending our country, but because I considered that conscription, far from promoting voluntary enlistment, would hamper it. That is why, for the last twenty-five years, even during the last war, I have declared myself against conscription as being conscientiously opposed to that measure as I still am to-day.
Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec has contributed its large share in the present conflict and there are reasons to be proud of that province, proud of its citizens. Our province is sometimes criticized in this house by members who have not resided very long in Canada, but have come from the other side because, over there, they felt like small fish in a large lake. They came to Canada, where they settled and were welcomed by the Canadians who helped them to succeed and to-day they want.to show us how to run the country and the war. Mr. Speaker, if those people are well intentioned why do they not set an example instead of always criticizing the province of Quebec? Even in this house, there are people of military age who could do their duty by returning overseas as sincere men. They could at least cease criticizing the honest people of Quebec who do their duty courageously and proudly.
I have always lived in the province of Quebec which I hold to be one of the finest provinces in Canada. I am proud to live among Canadians whom I esteem and I hope to have the privilege of spending there my remaining days.
I shall conclude in saying that the repeal of clause 3 will enable any government in power to enforce conscription without consulting even the house and that is why I shall vote against this bill.
On motion of Mr. Fraser (Northumberland, Ont.) the debate was adjourned.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
